The administrator posts a nondiscrimination notice with taglines in the office and includes it in the client admission packet. Taglines cover Spanish, Haitian Creole and the other languages most common in the agency's service area, as identified from local data.

At the first contact, the intake coordinator asks every client and representative their preferred language for spoken and written communication and whether they need any auxiliary aid. The answer is recorded on the intake form.

Before accepting the client, the intake coordinator and RN supervisor confirm that the agency can communicate with the client through a same-language staff person, an interpreter or translation technology and can assure all assigned visits (Rule 59A-8.020(1)).

If a same-language caregiver is not available, the language access coordinator arranges a qualified interpreter or translation technology before the first visit and documents the method. The agency does not decline a client solely because of the language they speak.
If communication cannot be arranged, the intake coordinator documents the efforts made and refers the person to other providers. The administrator reviews and approves every such decision.

The agency does not require or ask a client to provide their own interpreter. A family member or friend may interpret only if the client requests it, and the request is documented. A minor child may not interpret except in an emergency with no alternative.

The agency translates vital documents, including the service agreement (CR-06), the rights notice (CR-01), the hotline notices (CR-07), the grievance procedure (CR-02) and the privacy notice (CR-03), into the client's language or provides them orally through an interpreter. The agency documents that it did so.

For clients with disabilities, the intake coordinator provides reasonable modifications and auxiliary aids, such as large print, extra time, and sign language interpreters, and records them in the plan of care.

The scheduler matches caregivers to clients with consideration of language and documented cultural preferences, and does not reject a client because of a protected characteristic. Clients may ask for a different caregiver, and the request is not held against them.

The agency trains employees on nondiscrimination, use of interpreters and cultural differences in families at orientation and annual in-service (PER-03), consistent with aide training under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)13, F.A.C.

Employees must not make discriminatory comments, refuse care because of a protected status, or give a lower standard of care. A violation is reported to the administrator the same day and is addressed under PER-09.

Complaints of discrimination are handled under CR-02. The administrator tracks them and reports them to the QA committee (GOV-04). The administrator refers any complaint to the appropriate state or federal civil rights agency when required. No client or employee is retaliated against for raising a concern.
The administrator reviews language service use, requests for aids, and discrimination complaints at least annually and updates the interpreter list, taglines and training.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance, designates the language access coordinator, reviews any refusal of a client, and reports to QA.
Maintains the interpreter and bilingual staff lists, arranges interpreters and translations, and tracks language service use.
Asks language and aid preferences, confirms communication access before acceptance, and documents the method.
Confirms communication capability in the assessment and plan of care.
Treat all clients equally, use the arranged language services, and report discrimination concerns.

documentation: Intake form showing preferred language and aid needs
Record of interpreter or translation method for each client
Translated vital documents and proof of delivery
Posted nondiscrimination notice and tagline copies
Interpreter vendor and bilingual staff list
Training records
Discrimination complaint file and annual review summary

policies.title: Written Service Agreement, Rates and Billing Disclosure
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, administrator, RN supervisors, billing staff and scheduler
policies.purpose: To ensure every client and representative understands in writing what services will be provided, what they will cost, and who pays before services begin.
policies.policy: Before services start, [AGENCY NAME] executes a written agreement with each client that lists the services to be provided, the rates or charges for privately paid services, and the sources of payment: Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, personal funds or a combination (s. 400.487(1), F.S.). The agreement is signed and dated by an agency representative and by the client or legal representative. The client receives a copy, and the original is kept in the client file (Rule 59A-8.020(2), F.A.C.). For aide, homemaker and companion clients without a treatment order, the agreement is the service provision plan (Rule 59A-8.020(3)).

definitions.definition: The signed document listing services, rates, payment sources and the terms of care between the agency and the client.
For aide, homemaker and companion clients with no treatment order, the service agreement serves as the plan, as set by Rule 59A-8.020(3).
A person with legal authority to sign for the client, such as a guardian, health care surrogate or agent under a power of attorney. Staff verify and copy the authority document.
A service paid by the client or family from personal funds or private insurance, as opposed to Medicaid or another public program.

procedures: After the assessment and acceptance decision (SVC-02), the intake coordinator prepares the service agreement for the client before the first scheduled visit. No services begin until the agreement is signed.
The agreement lists each service to be provided, such as personal care, homemaker or companion services, and the frequency, days and hours of service. It must match the plan of care (SVC-03).

The agreement states the hourly rate or charge for each privately paid service, including any different rates for nights, weekends and holidays, mileage, and any other fee. It states the minimum shift length.

The agreement identifies each payment source: Medicare, Medicaid or a managed care plan, private insurance, personal funds, or a mix. For public-payer clients, it states the authorized hours and any client share.
The agreement describes the billing cycle, invoice delivery, payment due date, accepted payment methods and the process to dispute a charge. It names the billing contact at [PHONE].
The agreement states the cancellation terms, including the notice a client must give and any charge for late cancellations. It states what the agency will do to cover a missed visit (SVC-08).

The agreement states the charge, if any, for RN supervisory visits. Under s. 400.487(3), F.S., these visits are arranged per the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay for them, and the agreement documents the client's decision. It also includes the client's written consent for the RN to enter the home (Rule 59A-8.0095(3)(c), F.A.C.).

The agreement states the termination terms for both parties, including the notice period, the refund of any prepaid amounts, and the right to receive written notice of the date and reason for discharge (SVC-11).

The intake coordinator reviews the agreement with the client or representative in plain language and in their preferred language or with an interpreter (CR-05). The client may ask questions and may take time to consider.
The client or legal representative and an agency representative sign and date the agreement. If a representative signs, staff copy the document establishing authority and place it in the file.

The intake coordinator gives the client a copy at signing and places the original in the client file. For a client with no treatment order, it is kept for one year after termination of services (Rule 59A-8.020(3)).

The intake coordinator also tells the client that they may receive a copy of the plan of care on request and may participate in care planning (s. 400.487(4), F.S.), and documents that this was explained.

Rate or service changes are made only by written amendment signed by the client or representative. The agency gives written notice of rate increases at least 30 days before they take effect, and the client may end services without penalty.

The billing staff bill only for services documented as delivered, using verified time records (SVC-09), and give itemized invoices at the client's request. Billing errors are corrected and credited within 30 days of discovery.
The administrator audits a sample of new agreements each month to confirm they are complete, signed, dated and consistent with billing, and reports the results to QA (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Prepares and explains the agreement, obtains signatures, delivers the client copy and files the original.
Approves the agreement template and rates, audits agreements, and signs as agency representative or delegates in writing.
Ensures services listed match the assessment and plan of care and documents the client's consent for supervisory visits.
Bills according to the agreement and verified visit records and resolves billing disputes.

documentation: Signed and dated service agreement, original in the client file
Proof the client received a copy
Copy of the legal representative's authority document, if applicable
Written consent for RN home entry and supervisory visit decision
Signed amendments and rate-change notices
Billing and invoice records
Monthly agreement audit results

policies.title: Required Notices: Complaint, Abuse and Medicaid Fraud Hotlines
policies.applies_to: Intake coordinator, administrator, RN supervisors, and any staff who start services for a client
policies.purpose: To make sure every client knows how to report a complaint, abuse, neglect, exploitation or suspected Medicaid fraud before services begin, as the law requires.
policies.policy: On or before the first day of service, [AGENCY NAME] gives each client and, if appropriate, the client's immediate family or representative three written notices (s. 408.810(5)(a), F.S.). The first is the AHCA complaint number with the words "To report a complaint regarding the services you receive, please call toll-free [AHCA COMPLAINT HOTLINE NUMBER]." The second is the central abuse hotline with the words "To report abuse, neglect, or exploitation, please call toll-free 1-800-962-2873." The third is an agency-written description of Medicaid fraud with the words "To report suspected Medicaid fraud, please call toll-free [MEDICAID FRAUD HOTLINE NUMBER]." The notices are clearly legible, and this policy is the agency's written procedure for delivering them (s. 408.810(5)(b), F.S.).

definitions.definition: The Florida Abuse Hotline operated by the Department of Children and Families, 1-800-962-2873, which receives reports of abuse, neglect and exploitation.
The toll-free number published by the Agency for Health Care Administration for complaints about licensed providers. The administrator keeps the current number in the notice template.

Intentional deception or misrepresentation to obtain a Medicaid payment to which one is not entitled, such as billing for services not given. The agency's written description is included in the notice.
A person legally authorized to act for the client, or a family member the client has designated to receive information.

procedures: The administrator keeps a single Required Hotline Notice with the three statements above. It includes the agency's plain-language description of Medicaid fraud, and it is printed in clear, legible type.

Before the notice is used, the administrator enters the AHCA complaint number and the Medicaid fraud number currently published by AHCA. The administrator confirms them against AHCA's published numbers at least every six months and whenever AHCA announces a change.

If AHCA announces a number change, the administrator updates the notice template within the notice period (AHCA gives a minimum of 90 days) and removes old copies from admission packets and the office.

The intake coordinator places the notice in each client's admission packet and schedules its delivery for on or before the first day of service. Services may not start until delivery is documented, and no later than the first visit.
The intake coordinator or RN supervisor gives the notice to the client and, if appropriate, to the client's immediate family or representative, and explains each hotline in plain language.

If the client has limited English proficiency, a visual or hearing impairment or limited literacy, staff provide the notice in the client's language or an accessible format, or read it aloud through an interpreter (CR-05).
The client or representative signs and dates the Notice Acknowledgment. If the client cannot sign, staff note the reason and the date of delivery, and a second staff member witnesses it.
The intake coordinator gives the client a copy of the notice to keep and files the signed acknowledgment in the client record as proof of delivery (REC-01).

The administrator confirms at the pre-service chart check that each new client's file contains a signed acknowledgment dated on or before the first day of service. A missing acknowledgment is corrected the same day and noted as a QA finding.
When notices are changed, the administrator sends the updated notice to all active clients, with documentation, at the next supervisory visit or within 30 days, whichever comes first.

Staff tell clients that they may report to any hotline at any time without fear of retaliation and without first going through the agency (CR-01, CR-02). Staff who see or suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation must also follow SAF-01.
The administrator audits acknowledgment records quarterly and reports compliance rates to the QA committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the notice template and current numbers, audits delivery, and corrects any gaps.
Packages, delivers and explains the notice and obtains the signed acknowledgment on or before the first day of service.
Confirms delivery at the assessment and re-delivers or explains again on request.
Answer client questions about the hotlines and report abuse, neglect or exploitation under SAF-01.

documentation: Current Required Hotline Notice with version date
Signed Notice Acknowledgment for each client
Record of verification of the AHCA numbers
Record of notice updates sent to clients
Quarterly audit report

policies.title: Advance Directives and Do-Not-Resuscitate Orders
policies.applies_to: All clinical and direct care staff, intake coordinator, RN supervisors and administrator
policies.purpose: To respect each client's right to make decisions about their medical care and to make sure staff know how to respond when a valid advance directive or DNR order exists.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects a client's right to accept or refuse care and to make advance directives. Home health agency personnel may withhold or withdraw cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) when presented with a do-not-resuscitate (DNR) order executed under s. 401.45, F.S. They are protected from criminal prosecution and civil liability for doing so (s. 400.487(7), F.S.). A client's decision about an advance directive or DNR is never a condition of receiving services. Without a valid DNR order presented, staff call 911 in an emergency and begin CPR if they hold current certification.

definitions.definition: A written or oral statement of a person's wishes about future medical care, such as a living will or designation of a health care surrogate.
A physician's order, executed under s. 401.45, F.S., directing that CPR be withheld if a person's breathing or heart stops.
A person the client has designated, or the law recognizes, to make health care decisions if the client cannot.
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation, the emergency effort to restore breathing and circulation.

procedures: At intake, the intake coordinator or RN supervisor asks each client or representative whether the client has an advance directive, a health care surrogate designation or a DNR order. The answer is recorded on the intake form.
Staff tell the client that the agency will respect these decisions, that having or not having one will not affect access to services, and that the agency will not make the decision for them.

If the client has none and asks for information, the RN supervisor provides general written information and refers the client to their physician or an attorney. Staff do not give legal or medical advice and do not witness advance directives.

If the client has a document, the intake coordinator makes a copy, confirms it is signed and dated, and files it in the client record. For a DNR order, the RN supervisor checks that it appears to be executed under s. 401.45, F.S.
The RN supervisor notes the DNR or directive in the plan of care and on the assignment sheet, so the assigned aide knows it before the first visit (SVC-03).

The RN supervisor tells the client and family where the original DNR order should be kept in the home, in a place visible and readily accessible to responders, and asks them to have it available at each visit.

The administrator verifies the current text of the state advance-directive rules for home health agencies before this policy is adopted and at each annual review, and updates these procedures if required.

If a client's heart or breathing stops and a valid DNR order is presented, the aide does not start CPR. The aide stays with the client, calls 911 or the number on the DNR instructions, shows the order to responders, and notifies the RN supervisor.

If no valid DNR order is presented, the aide calls 911 immediately and starts CPR if the aide is trained and holds current CPR certification (SVC-10). Staff do not search for a DNR order while delaying emergency care.

For any other emergency, such as a fall, choking or chest pain, aides call 911 unless the client's plan states a different approach. A DNR order covers CPR only and does not prevent calls for other emergency help.
Staff report any dispute between family members and the DNR or directive to the RN supervisor and the administrator, and follow the order presented. The agency does not resolve legal disputes.
The aide documents the event and actions taken, and the RN supervisor completes an incident report within 24 hours (SAF-02).

If the client revokes or changes a directive or DNR, the representative or the client informs the RN supervisor, who updates the record and the plan of care and replaces superseded copies the same day.
The agency trains staff on this policy at orientation and annual in-service (PER-03), including the importance of current CPR certification.
If the agency becomes certified for Medicare or Medicaid, the administrator reviews the federal advance-directive requirements for participating providers and amends this policy before certification.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the policy is current, verifies the applicable rule text, and reviews incidents.
Reviews documents, updates the plan of care, informs aides, and completes incident follow-up.
Asks about directives at intake and files copies.
Knows if a client has a DNR order, responds as set out here, calls 911 and documents.

documentation: Intake form noting directive and DNR status
Copy of advance directive, surrogate designation or DNR order
Plan of care and assignment sheet notation
Incident report and visit notes of any event
Training records

policies.title: Scope of Services: Personal Care vs. Homemaker and Companion
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN supervisors, intake coordinator, scheduler, home health aides/CNAs, homemakers and companions
policies.purpose: To define what services [AGENCY NAME] provides, what each type of caregiver may and may not do, and what is outside the agency's license or registration.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides only non-skilled services within the scope of its home health agency license limited to non-skilled services and, where applicable, its homemaker and companion registration. Home health aides provide hands-on personal care. Companions and homemakers may not provide hands-on personal care (s. 400.462, F.S.). Aides and CNAs do not perform skilled tasks. The agency does not provide nursing or therapy services unless its license is amended to add skilled care. Staff are assigned only tasks within their role and written assignment.

definitions.definition: Hands-on assistance with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, eating, hygiene and transfers, as defined in s. 400.462, F.S.
An employee who meets the certification and training requirements of Rule 59A-8.0095(5), F.A.C., and provides hands-on personal care under RN supervision.
A person who provides home upkeep, meals, laundry, shopping, household chores and casual cosmetic help, without hands-on personal care (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)(a)).

A person who provides companionship, escort to appointments or outings, light housekeeping, a chronological written record of services and cosmetic help, without hands-on personal care (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)(b)).
A task that requires nursing or other licensed clinical skill, such as sterile dressings or catheterization, and that aides, homemakers and companions may not perform.

procedures: The administrator ensures the license application states explicitly which services are provided directly by employees and which are provided by contract, and that at least one service is provided directly to clients (Rule 59A-8.008(4), F.A.C.). The administrator updates the statement whenever the arrangement changes.

The intake coordinator and RN supervisor review each referral against this policy before acceptance. A request for skilled care, or any other service outside the license, is declined, and the person is referred to an appropriately licensed provider (SVC-02, SVC-11).
For clients who need hands-on help, the RN supervisor assigns a home health aide or CNA. A homemaker or companion is never assigned to any task that involves hands-on personal care.

Home health aides and CNAs may perform personal hygiene, ambulation, eating, dressing, shaving and physical transfers, light housekeeping and laundry, and other tasks given in a written assignment from a licensed professional (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l)).
Homemakers may perform home upkeep, meal preparation, laundry, shopping, household chores and casual cosmetic help (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)(a)).

Companions may provide companionship, escort the client to appointments or outings, perform light housekeeping and give cosmetic help. They keep a chronological written record of the services they provide (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)(b)).

Homemakers and companions may help a walking client stabilize by holding an arm or hand only. They may not lift, transfer, bathe, dress, toilet or feed a client. Their only medication role is a verbal reminder that it is time to take medicine, and only at the client's request.

Aides and CNAs may not perform sterile dressings, enemas, wound irrigation or debridement, gastric or enteral feeding, catheterizing, administration of Schedule II-IV controlled substances, application of heat, tracheostomy care, or filling or removing medications from a pill organizer or dispenser (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(p)).

Medication assistance by an aide follows SVC-06 and s. 400.488, F.S., which allows unlicensed assistance only for medically stable clients with routine, regularly scheduled medications, a documented request and written informed consent. Other tasks such as glucometer use, antiembolism stockings, oxygen, CPAP, vital signs and colostomy bags follow SVC-07. Aides do none of the exclusions listed in s. 400.488(4), F.S.
The RN supervisor writes each client's task list in the plan of care (SVC-03), naming the caregiver type and the tasks, and gives the assigned caregiver a copy before the first visit.

If a caregiver is asked by a client or family to perform a task outside the plan of care or outside the caregiver's role, the caregiver politely declines, explains it is outside the agency's scope, and calls the RN supervisor the same day. The RN supervisor decides whether the plan can be changed within scope or the client needs another provider.

If a client's needs change so that a homemaker or companion client now needs hands-on help, the RN supervisor arranges an assessment, an updated agreement and plan, and a home health aide assignment before any hands-on care starts (SVC-03).

If a client's needs become skilled, the RN supervisor notifies the client and representative and the physician or payer when appropriate, helps arrange care from a skilled provider, and follows the discharge or transfer procedure (SVC-10, SVC-11).

An agency that contracts directly with an assisted living facility or adult family care home resident coordinates with the facility and keeps responsibility for its own services (Rule 59A-8.008(5)). If the agency's office is in space inside an assisted living facility, the administrator notifies AHCA in writing (Rule 59A-8.008(6)).

Scope violations are reported by caregivers to the RN supervisor and by the RN supervisor to the administrator the same day. The administrator documents corrective action, such as retraining or discipline, and reports the findings to QA (GOV-04).
The administrator reviews this policy annually and when the license, registration or rules change, and trains staff on the scope of their role at orientation and annual in-service (PER-03).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the license scope, the service and contract statement, and compliance with this policy; handles scope violations.
Assigns caregivers by role, writes the task list, and decides on requests outside scope.
Screens referrals for services within scope and refers out those that are not.
Performs only assigned tasks within Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l) and refuses excluded tasks.
Provides only non-hands-on services, keeps the chronological record, and calls the RN supervisor if hands-on help is needed.

documentation: License application statement of direct and contracted services
Referral screening note with acceptance or referral-out decision
Plan of care task list and caregiver assignment sheet
Companion chronological service record
Scope-violation report and corrective action
Training records
Annual policy review record

policies.title: Client Intake, Acceptance and Assessment
policies.applies_to: Administrator, alternate administrator, RN supervisor, intake/scheduling staff. Applies to every prospective client of the agency's non-skilled home health aide (personal care), homemaker and companion services.
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] accepts only clients whose needs it can safely meet in the home, collects the client information Florida requires, and begins each client relationship with a documented assessment and a signed written agreement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts a client only when there is a reasonable expectation that the client's needs can be met adequately and safely in the client's place of residence (Rule 59A-8.020(1)). This includes the ability to communicate with the client through a same-language staff person, an interpreter or translation technology. The agency accepts a client only when it can supply capable employees or contractors for all assigned visits. Where the agency operates under a Homemaker and Companion registration, the same standard applies under Rule 59A-8.025(9). The agency provides no skilled services. A person whose needs require skilled nursing or therapy is referred elsewhere. Before or at the start of services, the RN supervisor performs an intake assessment of the client's home, abilities and needs. The agency also collects the client record information required by Rule 59A-8.025(8). A written agreement signed and dated by an agency representative and the client or representative is completed before services start.

definitions.definition: A person who receives or is being considered for aide (personal care), homemaker or companion services from the agency.

A documented review, led by the RN supervisor, of the client's needs, abilities, home environment, safety risks and communication needs, used to decide whether the agency can accept the client and to prepare the task list.
A legal guardian, health care surrogate, attorney-in-fact or other person lawfully authorized to act for the client.
For aide, homemaker and companion clients with no treatment order, the signed written agreement serves as the plan (see SVC-03).

procedures: Intake staff record every inquiry on the intake log on the day received: date, caller, referral source, requested services, requested start date and preferred language.

Intake staff screen the request against SVC-01. A request for skilled nursing, therapy, injections, wound care or other skilled tasks is declined and the caller is referred to a licensed skilled provider. The referral is logged.

Intake staff confirm the requested service type. Hands-on personal care is accepted only under the Home Health Agency license. If the agency holds only a Homemaker and Companion registration, any request for hands-on help is declined and referred.

The administrator or intake staff identify the client's language and communication needs at first contact and record them. The agency confirms that a same-language staff person, an interpreter or translation technology (see CR-05) is available before accepting.

The RN supervisor completes an intake assessment before services begin, or at the start of services if the client's urgent need requires it. The assessment is performed in the client's residence unless the client cannot be met there before the start date, in which case the RN completes it at the first visit. The assessment covers the client's functional abilities, personal care needs, cognitive status, home safety, fall and fire hazards, pets, smoking, firearms, availability of family or other caregivers, and any medication or other-task assistance requested (SVC-06, SVC-07).

Before accepting, the RN supervisor and scheduler confirm that qualified aides are available for every visit requested, on the days, hours and in the area requested. If the agency cannot supply capable staff for all assigned visits, the agency does not accept the client and refers the client elsewhere.

Intake staff collect and enter in the confidential client record: full legal name, address, telephone number, age, the basis for the disability or need for service, emergency contact, next of kin or guardian, physician, diet restrictions, food allergies and activity limitations (Rule 59A-8.025(8)).

If the client lives in an assisted living facility or adult family care home, the administrator or RN supervisor contacts the facility before the first visit. The agency coordinates its services with the facility, identifies the services the facility is already obligated to provide, avoids duplicating them, and remains responsible for the services the agency provides.

The RN supervisor decides on acceptance based on the assessment. If the RN judges that services cannot be provided safely, the client is not accepted. The reason is documented and the client is given referral information.

The RN supervisor documents the acceptance decision, the assessment findings and the task list (see SVC-03). The RN also records any condition that must be reported to the client's physician or other provider.

The agreement is prepared according to CR-06 and states the services, the rates for privately paid services and the payment sources. An agency representative and the client or representative review it with the client in a language and manner the client understands.
The client or representative and an agency representative sign and date the agreement. The client receives a copy at signing and the original is placed in the client file (Rule 59A-8.020(2)).

At or before the first visit, the agency gives the client the required notices, including complaint and abuse hotline information (CR-07), the Client Rights statement (CR-01) and the privacy notice (CR-03). It also obtains the client's written consent for the RN to enter the home for supervisory visits (SVC-04).
The scheduler assigns an aide who has the training and competencies required for the client's task list (PER-01, PER-03). The scheduler gives the aide the task list before the first visit.
If the client later seeks services the agency cannot provide, or the client's condition exceeds the agency's scope, the RN supervisor follows SVC-10 and SVC-11.
The administrator reviews the intake log and a sample of intake files at least quarterly as part of Quality Assurance (GOV-04) to confirm complete documentation and compliance with this policy.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures that only clients who can be served safely are accepted, that capable staff are available for all assigned visits, and that intake records are complete.
Performs the intake assessment, decides on acceptance on clinical grounds, prepares the task list and documents findings.
Log inquiries, screen requests for scope, collect client record information, confirm staff availability and communication access, and prepare agreements for signature.
Performs these duties when the administrator is unavailable.

documentation: Intake log
Intake assessment and acceptance/decline decision, signed and dated by the RN
Confidential client record containing the Rule 59A-8.025(8) items
Written agreement signed and dated by the agency representative and client or representative (original in the client file, copy to client)
Record of language/interpreter arrangements
Referral log for declined clients
Record of coordination with the ALF or adult family care home, if applicable

policies.title: Service Provision Plan / Plan of Care and Plan Updates
policies.applies_to: Administrator, RN supervisor, scheduling staff, home health aides/CNAs, homemakers and companions.
policies.purpose: To establish how [AGENCY NAME] documents the services each client will receive, informs clients of their right to take part in planning, and keeps the plan current.
policies.policy: For aide, homemaker and companion clients who have no treatment order, the signed written agreement is the service provision plan (Rule 59A-8.020(3)). [AGENCY NAME] supplements the agreement with an RN-prepared task list for clients who receive aide services. A plan of care developed in consultation with a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse is required only for skilled care (s. 400.487(2); Rule 59A-8.0215(1)), and the agency provides no skilled services. The client or guardian is told that the client has the right to be informed of the plan, to take part in developing it and to receive a copy on request (s. 400.487(4); Rule 59A-8.0215(3)). The plan is reviewed at each RN supervisory visit and whenever the client's condition or needs change, and changes are recorded in the client file. Staff provide only the services listed in the plan.

definitions.definition: The signed and dated written agreement that identifies the services to be provided to an aide, homemaker or companion client who has no treatment order.
An RN-prepared, client-specific list of the personal care tasks an aide is assigned to perform, including how and when, and any limits or precautions.
A physician, PA or APRN order for skilled services. Skilled services are not provided by this agency.
The plan developed with a physician, PA or APRN for skilled care. It applies to this agency only if a client's order for skilled care is referred out.

procedures: At intake, the RN supervisor confirms whether the client has a treatment order for skilled care. If the client needs skilled care, the agency does not accept the client for that care and refers the client under SVC-02 and SVC-11.

For clients without a treatment order, the intake staff and the client or representative prepare the written agreement (see CR-06). It names the services, schedule, rates for private-pay services and payment sources, and serves as the service provision plan.

For aide clients, the RN supervisor prepares the client-specific task list from the intake assessment. The list identifies each task, special instructions, precautions, and tasks the aide must not perform. It also identifies any medication assistance or other-task assistance the client has consented to (SVC-06, SVC-07).

The RN supervisor reviews the agreement and task list with the client or representative before services begin. The RN uses plain language and the client's preferred language, and invites the client's input on tasks, preferences, routines and schedule.
The RN or intake staff tell the client or guardian, orally and in the written agreement, that the client may be informed of the plan, take part in developing it, and receive a copy on request.

The client or representative and the agency representative sign and date the agreement. The client is given a copy of the agreement and, on request, a copy of the task list. A request for a copy is documented and fulfilled promptly, no later than the next business day.

The scheduler gives the assigned aide the task list before the first visit. The RN confirms that the aide understands the list and is qualified for each task (SVC-04). Homemakers and companions receive a list of homemaker and companion tasks only.

Aides, homemakers and companions perform only the tasks in the plan. A staff member must not perform a personal health service that is not in the plan, even at the client's or family's request. The staff member reports the request to the RN supervisor the same day.

At each RN supervisory visit, the RN reviews the plan and task list with the client and, where appropriate, the aide. The RN confirms the tasks remain appropriate and the client's wishes are met, and documents the review.

The RN supervisor reviews and updates the plan whenever the client's condition changes, the client or family asks for a change, an aide reports a change, or a hospitalization, fall or incident occurs (SVC-10, SAF-02).
Any change in services, schedule, rates or payment source is documented in writing. The client or representative signs and dates the revised agreement or an addendum, and receives a copy.

The RN supervisor documents each plan change in the client file, including the date, the reason, who was consulted and who approved it. The updated task list goes to the aide before the next visit. Staff receive the update by telephone or in person if the next visit is imminent, and the update is documented.
If a client's needs grow beyond what the agency's non-skilled services can safely meet, the RN supervisor notifies the administrator and begins the referral and discharge process (SVC-11).

The administrator reviews a sample of plans and task lists at least quarterly as part of Quality Assurance (GOV-04). The review checks that agreements are signed, task lists are current and plan changes are recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Prepares and reviews the task list, reviews the plan at each supervisory visit and on any change in condition, explains the client's right to take part in planning, and documents updates.
Ensures every client has a signed agreement and a current task list and that the plan process is followed.
Prepare agreements and revisions, distribute task lists and copies to aides and clients, and file signed documents.
Perform only the services in the plan, and report changes or requests for additional tasks to the RN supervisor the same day.

documentation: Signed and dated written agreement (service provision plan) and addenda
RN-prepared task list for each aide client with revision dates
Record that the client or guardian was told of the right to be informed of, participate in and receive a copy of the plan
Record of copies provided on request
RN supervisory visit notes showing plan review
Documentation of every plan change and who was notified
Quarterly QA review findings

policies.title: RN Supervision, Task Assignment and Supervisory Visits
policies.applies_to: Administrator, alternate administrator, RN supervisors, home health aides/CNAs and scheduling staff.
policies.purpose: To ensure that every aide who provides hands-on personal care for [AGENCY NAME] is assigned tasks by, and supervised by, a registered nurse who is accountable for that care.
policies.policy: A registered nurse who holds a current Florida license or an active multistate license assigns personal care tasks to aides and CNAs and maintains full responsibility for those tasks. The RN makes sure each aide is qualified for each assignment by training and experience (Rule 59A-8.0095(3)(b)). The agency arranges RN supervisory visits of aides in the client's home, as required by s. 400.487(3) and Rule 59A-8.0095(3)(c). These visits are made in accordance with the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay for them. The agency obtains the written consent of the client, guardian or representative before an RN enters the home. The RN provides on-site supervision as needed, based on the severity of the client's medical condition and the aide's training and experience (Rule 59A-8.0095(3)(d)). Because Florida rules set no fixed frequency, the RN decides the frequency for each client and documents the rationale. Although an agency with no skilled care is not required to employ a director of nursing (Rule 59A-8.0095(2)(i)), an RN must still provide supervisory visits.

definitions.definition: A registered nurse, licensed in Florida or holding an active multistate license, who assigns tasks to and supervises aides for the agency.
A visit by the RN to the client's home to observe and supervise aide services, review the plan, and check the client's satisfaction and safety.
Home health aides, CNAs and other staff who are not licensed nurses and who provide personal care under RN supervision.
The written consent of the client, guardian or representative for the agency's RN to enter the home.

procedures: At hire and annually, the administrator verifies that each RN supervisor holds a current Florida RN license or an active multistate license (verified on the Department of Health license lookup), and files the verification in the personnel record (PER-07).

At intake, the RN supervisor obtains the client's or representative's written consent for the RN to enter the home for supervisory visits. The agency does not make a supervisory visit before consent is on file.

At intake, the RN supervisor explains that supervisory visits are made according to the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay. The RN supervisor records the client's decisions and the agreement on payment in the written agreement (CR-06).

Before assigning any task, the RN reviews the aide's file for current CNA certification or proof of the required 40 hours of training or passed competency test, current CPR, in-service hours and any medication-assistance training (PER-01, PER-03, PER-04, PER-05). The RN assigns only tasks for which the aide is qualified by training and experience.
The RN prepares the client-specific task list (SVC-03) and communicates the assignment to the aide before the first visit. The RN documents the assignment and who received it.

The RN determines the schedule and type of supervisory contact for each client. The RN bases this on the severity of the client's medical condition, the complexity of tasks, the aide's training and experience, any new aide assignment, and client or family concerns. The rationale is documented in the client file.

As a minimum agency standard, the RN makes a supervisory visit with a new aide or a new client assignment within [AGENCY STANDARD: number] days of the start of service. The RN also makes follow-up visits at the interval recorded in the client file. The administrator approves the agency standard in writing.

During each visit, the RN observes the aide performing tasks when the aide is present. The RN checks technique, infection control, safety, adherence to the task list and conduct. The RN also checks the client's condition, home safety and client satisfaction, and reviews the plan (SVC-03).
If an aide is not present at the visit, the RN reviews the aide's documentation, speaks with the client, and schedules an observed visit as soon as practical.

The RN gives the aide immediate feedback and, where needed, retrains the aide on site. If the RN finds a performance or safety problem, the RN documents it, restricts or removes the task assignment if necessary, and informs the administrator the same day.

The RN documents every supervisory visit in the client file on the day of the visit. The note includes date, time, those present, observations, findings, client comments, actions taken, plan changes and follow-up needed.
When the RN identifies a change in the client's condition, the RN follows SVC-10 and notifies the client's physician or other provider and the client's representative as appropriate.

The RN supervisor remains fully responsible for the tasks the RN assigns. An aide may not assign tasks to another aide, and an LPN or other staff member may not substitute for the RN's assignment decision.
The RN reviews each aide's competency at least annually and whenever a performance concern arises. Unsatisfactory findings are handled under PER-03.
The administrator tracks supervisory visit completion monthly and reports it to the QA committee (GOV-04). Missed or late visits are investigated and corrected.
Supervision applies to personal care services. Homemakers and companions, who provide no hands-on help, receive supervision from the administrator or designee as described in SVC-01 and PER-09.

responsibilities.duty: Assigns tasks, confirms aide qualifications, makes and documents supervisory visits, and remains fully responsible for assigned tasks.
Employs or contracts qualified RNs, verifies licensure, ensures client consent for RN entry is on file, and tracks supervisory visit completion.
Perform only assigned tasks, accept RN direction, and promptly report changes, problems or tasks they are not trained to do.
Schedule supervisory visits and notify clients and aides in advance.

documentation: RN license verification
Client's written consent for RN entry into the home
Written agreement showing the client's direction, approval and agreement to pay for supervisory visits
Task assignment record with aide qualification check
RN supervisory visit notes
Rationale for supervision frequency in the client file
Aide annual competency evaluations
Monthly supervisory visit tracking report

policies.title: RN Supervisor Availability During Hours of Client Service
policies.applies_to: Administrator, alternate administrator, RN supervisors, aides/CNAs, homemakers, companions and scheduling staff.
policies.purpose: To make sure aides and clients can reach a registered nurse supervisor whenever [AGENCY NAME] staff are providing client services, as Florida requires of a home health agency that does not provide skilled services.
policies.policy: A home health agency that does not provide skilled services must have written policies and procedures addressing the availability of a registered nurse supervisor during hours of patient service (Rule 59A-8.003(9)(d)). [AGENCY NAME] provides no skilled care. It therefore does not maintain the 24-hour on-call system required of skilled agencies. However, an RN supervisor or backup RN is reachable by telephone during every hour that any aide, homemaker or companion is scheduled to serve a client. The agency states its hours of client service, publishes the RN contact number to staff and clients, and documents each contact. In an emergency, staff call 911 first and then notify the RN.

definitions.definition: Any time an agency employee or contractor is scheduled to be, or is, in a client's home providing services, including evenings, weekends and holidays.
The registered nurse responsible for supervising aides (SVC-04).
A second qualified RN designated in writing to cover when the primary RN supervisor is unavailable.
Nursing, therapy and other services requiring a license and a treatment order. The agency does not provide them.

procedures: The administrator defines in writing the agency's hours of client service, based on the current schedule of aide, homemaker and companion visits, and updates the schedule whenever hours change. The RN coverage schedule must match those hours.

The administrator designates a primary RN supervisor and at least one backup RN, by name, license number and telephone number, for all hours of client service. Both are listed on the weekly RN coverage schedule.
The scheduler posts the RN coverage schedule weekly, and keeps it accessible to the administrator, alternate and all on-duty staff.

The agency maintains a dedicated RN contact telephone number, [PHONE]. A live RN, or a forwarding or answering system that reaches an RN, is staffed during all hours of client service. The number is given to every aide and posted on the aide's task list.

Each aide, homemaker and companion receives the RN contact number and the escalation process at orientation (PER-03) and again in writing whenever they change. Clients receive the number in the written agreement.

As an agency standard, the RN or the backup RN returns every call from an aide in the field as quickly as practical and within [AGENCY STANDARD: number] minutes. If the first RN does not respond within that time, the aide calls the backup RN and then the administrator or alternate.

If the aide believes the client is in immediate danger, such as unresponsive, not breathing, a serious fall, chest pain, stroke symptoms or severe bleeding, the aide calls 911 first and then notifies the RN supervisor (SVC-10).

If an aide cannot reach any RN, the aide does not perform a task outside the plan or beyond the aide's training. The aide stays with the client when safe and appropriate and continues calling the numbers on the coverage list. The aide notifies the administrator.
The RN who takes a call documents it the same day: date, time, caller, client, concern, the RN's advice and any follow-up, such as a visit or a call to the physician or representative.

When the RN advises, the RN advises only within the non-skilled scope of services and care plan. The RN does not direct skilled care. If a client needs skilled care, the RN follows SVC-10 and SVC-11 and arranges referral.

The administrator tests the RN contact system at least quarterly by placing a call at a random hour of service. Results are documented and failures are corrected within [AGENCY STANDARD: number] business days.
The administrator reviews RN contact logs monthly for response time, unresolved calls and trends, and reports to the QA committee (GOV-04).

When the primary RN is on leave or resigns, the administrator immediately names a replacement or interim coverage in writing and notifies staff before the change takes effect. The agency does not schedule client services during hours with no RN coverage.

responsibilities.duty: Defines hours of client service, designates the primary and backup RNs, ensures coverage for every hour of service, and monitors response.
Remain reachable during assigned hours, respond to staff calls, advise within scope, escalate emergencies and document each contact.
Know and use the RN contact number and escalation order, call 911 in emergencies, and report concerns promptly.
Build the weekly RN coverage schedule to match service hours and notify staff of changes.

documentation: Written statement of hours of client service
Weekly RN coverage schedule with primary and backup RN names and numbers
RN contact call log
Quarterly test of the RN contact system and corrective action
Orientation record showing staff received RN contact instructions
Monthly RN availability review in QA minutes

policies.title: Medication Assistance and Self-Administration Support
policies.applies_to: RN supervisors, home health aides/CNAs, homemakers, companions, scheduling staff and the administrator.
policies.purpose: To define the limited help with medication that unlicensed [AGENCY NAME] staff may give, and to protect clients by setting consent, training, supervision and recordkeeping requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] aides and CNAs may assist with self-administration of medication only for medically stable clients, only with routine, regularly scheduled medications, and only on a documented request and the client's written informed consent (s. 400.488(2)). A licensed health care professional must tell the client or caregiver that an unlicensed person may assist (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(n)). An RN reviews the client to confirm medical stability and reviews and reconciles all current prescribed and over-the-counter medications (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(m)). Only aides who have completed the required medication-assistance training and verified label reading may assist. Homemakers and companions may only give verbal reminders at the request of the client or responsible party. Staff never perform the assistance that Florida law excludes, and every assist is recorded.

definitions.definition: Limited help that lets a client who is able to take their own medication do so. The client remains the one who takes the medication.
A condition that does not require nursing supervision or judgment to manage the medications, as determined by the RN review.
A medication taken on a fixed schedule as stated on the label. It is not a PRN (as-needed) medication that requires judgment.
The client's signed written agreement for unlicensed staff to assist, given after being told that an unlicensed person will help.
The record in which the aide documents each time the aide assists with medication.

procedures: At intake, the RN supervisor asks whether the client wants help with medications and documents the client's or caregiver's request. Without a documented request, no assistance is given.

The RN reviews the client to confirm medical stability. The RN also reviews and reconciles all current prescribed and over-the-counter medications against labels and any physician list, and documents the review in the client file (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(m)). The RN resolves discrepancies with the client, caregiver or prescriber before any assistance is given.

If the client is not medically stable, or the medications are not routine and regularly scheduled, the RN does not authorize assistance. The RN documents the reason and discusses alternatives with the client, such as family help or referral to a licensed provider.
The RN, or another licensed health care professional, informs the client or caregiver that an unlicensed person may assist with medication, and documents it.

The client or representative signs a written informed consent for medication assistance. The consent is filed before the first assist. Consent is renewed if the client's medications or condition change significantly.

The RN verifies in the aide's personnel file that the aide has completed the 2-hour medication-assistance training required by Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)15, including state law and rules, procedures, common medications, and recognition of and response to side effects. The training must include a check that the aide can read medication labels. The RN does not assign medication assistance to an aide who cannot read labels or who lacks the training. Passing the competency test alone does not authorize medication assistance.
The RN lists medication assistance on the client's task list (SVC-03), specifying which medications, times and permitted help.

Permitted assistance (s. 400.488(3)): the aide brings the labeled container to the client, confirms that the medication is the client's, and orally advises the client of the medication's name and purpose. The aide may open the container and remove the prescribed amount and place an oral dose in the client's hand or in another container. The aide may apply topical medications, return the container to storage and assist with a nebulizer.

For supervision of self-administration, the aide's role is limited to obtaining the container, ensuring the medication is prescribed for the client, reminding the client that it is time to take it and observing the client take it (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l)6). Aides may not administer Schedule II-IV controlled substances.

Excluded tasks (s. 400.488(4)): aides do not mix or calculate doses, give injections, give medication through tubes or parenterally, perform irrigations, give rectal, urethral or vaginal preparations, or give PRN medications that require judgment. If the client asks for any of these, the aide declines and informs the RN the same day.
Homemakers and companions give only verbal reminders of medication time, at the client's or responsible party's request (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)). They do not handle, open or hand over medications.

If the aide sees an unclear label, a missing or wrong medication, an expired or damaged container, or a medication that does not match the list, the aide does not assist. The aide calls the RN and documents the event.

If the client refuses a medication, shows a reaction or side effect, or seems unwell after a dose, the aide does not force or give anything else. The aide follows SVC-10, calls the RN, and calls 911 if there is an emergency.

The aide records every assist in the medication assistance record at the time of the assist: date, time, medication name as labeled, what help was given, whether the client took it, refusals and observations (s. 400.488(3)).

The RN reviews medication assistance records and the reconciliation at each supervisory visit (SVC-04), and whenever the client's condition changes or the client has a hospital stay or new prescription. The RN documents the review.

A medication error or suspected error is reported to the RN immediately and documented under SAF-02. The RN notifies the prescriber as appropriate and the client's representative, and the administrator reviews it for corrective action.
The administrator verifies annually that each aide authorized to assist has current medication-assistance training and that the RN has retested label reading.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms medical stability, reconciles medications, ensures consent and notice are in the record, authorizes and supervises assistance, and reviews records.
Assist only within the permitted list after training, consent and RN authorization, refuse excluded tasks, and record each assist.
Give only verbal reminders at the request of the client or responsible party.
Ensures training, consent and recordkeeping are in place and that errors are reviewed.

documentation: Documented request for medication assistance
RN medical stability review and medication reconciliation
Client's signed written informed consent
Record that the client or caregiver was told an unlicensed person may assist
Aide training record showing 2-hour medication assistance course and label reading verification
Medication assistance record for each assist
RN review notes
Incident report for any medication error or refusal with consequences

policies.title: Assistance with Other Tasks (Glucometer, Stockings, Oxygen, CPAP, Vitals, Colostomy Bags)
policies.applies_to: RN supervisors, home health aides/CNAs and the administrator. Homemakers and companions may not perform these tasks.
policies.purpose: To state which additional tasks beyond routine personal care [AGENCY NAME] aides may perform, and the consent, training and plan requirements that apply.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] aides may assist with the following only on a documented request and the client's written informed consent, and only after training by the RN: using a glucometer for blood-glucose checks, putting on and taking off antiembolism stockings, applying and removing an oxygen cannula, assisting with a CPAP device, measuring vital signs, and assisting with colostomy bags (s. 400.488(2), (6)). Aides never titrate or change prescribed oxygen or CPAP settings. Tasks permitted under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l)3 must be taught for the specific client by a licensed health care professional and listed in the plan. Aides may not provide any personal health service that is not included in the plan of care or service plan (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(p)10).

definitions.definition: The tasks in s. 400.488(6): glucometer use, antiembolism stockings, oxygen cannula, CPAP, vital signs and colostomy bags.
Changing the flow rate, pressure or other prescribed setting of oxygen or CPAP equipment. Aides may not do this.
Instruction and demonstration by the RN for the specific client, followed by the RN's observation of the aide performing the task correctly.
Compression stockings prescribed for the client, which the aide may put on and take off but not fit, measure or adjust to treat a condition.

procedures: At intake or at any later request, the RN supervisor documents which of these tasks the client needs help with, who requested it and why. No task is performed without a documented request.

The RN confirms the task is within the permitted list in s. 400.488(6) or Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l)3, and that a prescriber's order, equipment instructions or the client's prescribed regimen already exist. The RN does not authorize any task that requires nursing judgment, such as interpreting results to adjust treatment.
The client or representative gives written informed consent for the specific task. The consent is filed in the client record before the aide first performs the task.

The RN teaches the aide the task for the specific client and equipment, observes the aide performing it correctly, and documents the training and the date. The aide does not perform the task until the RN approves in writing.

The RN lists each approved task in the client's task list or plan (SVC-03), including the frequency, the steps, the equipment, precautions and what to report. If a task is not on the plan, the aide does not do it (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(p)10).

Glucometer: the aide may perform the blood glucose check using the client's own meter after training. The aide records the reading, reports it to the RN, and reports any reading outside the range the RN has listed on the task list. The aide does not interpret the result, adjust medication or insulin, or give insulin.

Antiembolism stockings: the aide puts on and takes off the client's prescribed stockings as taught. The aide checks the skin and reports redness, swelling, pain, discoloration or breakdown to the RN the same day.

Oxygen cannula: the aide applies and removes the cannula at the flow rate prescribed and already set. The aide does not change the flow rate or titrate. The aide follows the oxygen safety rules for no smoking and open flames, and reports breathing difficulty, discomfort or equipment problems to the RN. If the client is in distress, the aide calls 911.

CPAP: the aide may help the client put on and remove the device and clean it per instructions. The aide does not adjust pressure or settings. The aide reports mask problems, skin irritation or the client's refusal to the RN.

Vital signs: the aide measures temperature, pulse, respirations and blood pressure with the equipment the RN has taught the aide to use, and records the values. The aide reports to the RN any value outside the parameters the RN has listed, and calls 911 if an emergency (SVC-10).

Colostomy bags: the aide may empty and change a colostomy bag, as taught for that client, maintaining privacy and infection control (SAF-03). The aide reports skin irritation, unusual output, bleeding, or an ill-fitting appliance to the RN. The aide does not perform stoma care that requires nursing judgment.

Other plan-listed tasks under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(l)3, such as bedpan and urinal help, non-invasive urinary devices, simple urine tests and intake and output, are performed only if taught for the client by the RN and listed in the plan.
The aide documents each task performed, including date, time, results or observations and any report to the RN, in the visit record.
The RN reviews task performance and records at each supervisory visit (SVC-04), re-observes the aide at least annually or when a concern arises, and updates or withdraws authorization as needed.

If a client requests any task not on the list, or a task that is excluded, the aide declines politely, explains that the agency cannot do it, and informs the RN the same day. The RN follows up with the client and, if appropriate, with referral to another provider.
The administrator reviews a sample of task records and consents at least quarterly as part of QA (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews each request, obtains consent, trains and observes the aide, lists approved tasks in the plan, and monitors performance.
Perform only approved tasks they have been trained for, never titrate settings, record results and report out-of-range values or concerns.
Ensures training, consent and documentation are in place and reviews compliance.

documentation: Documented request for each task
Client's written informed consent
RN training and competency observation record for each aide, client and task
Task list or plan showing approved tasks and parameters
Visit records showing each task performed and results
RN supervisory visit notes
Incident reports for any problem

policies.title: Scheduling, Missed Visits and Continuity of Care
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; all aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, schedulers and RN supervisors
policies.purpose: To make sure every client receives all of the visits the agency agreed to provide, that missed visits are handled quickly and safely, and that clients who depend on daily hands-on care keep continuous coverage during staff absences, emergencies and disasters.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts a client only when it can reasonably and safely provide the agreed services in the home and can assure that all assigned visits will be delivered (Rule 59A-8.020(1)). Registered homemaker and companion services will likewise be accepted only if the services can be provided adequately and safely, and the agency will supply capable staff for all visits (Rule 59A-8.025(9)). The agency will not accept a new client or add hours unless qualified staff are available for the full schedule. Every missed visit is treated as a service failure: the client is notified, a backup caregiver is sent when needed, the reason is documented, and the RN supervisor is notified for high-risk clients. Clients who depend on daily care, such as toileting, transfers, feeding or medication assistance, are identified at intake and have a written coverage plan for staff absence, emergencies and disasters (Rule 59A-8.027(9)-(10)).

definitions.definition: Any scheduled visit that is not started within the agency's late-arrival threshold of [30] minutes of the scheduled start time, is cut short without client agreement, or is not delivered at all, whatever the cause.

A client who needs hands-on help every day with tasks such as toileting, transfers, feeding, personal hygiene or medication assistance, so that a gap in service could create a risk to health or safety.

A client the RN supervisor identifies at intake or reassessment as likely to be harmed by a missed or late visit. Examples are a client who lives alone, has dementia, cannot summon help, is at high fall risk, or relies on the aide for medication help.
A qualified, screened and trained caregiver, whose training and competency are on file, who is available to cover a visit when the assigned caregiver cannot.
The written plan in the client's file that lists who covers the client's visits when the regular caregiver is absent and what happens during an emergency or disaster.

procedures: Before accepting a client, the Intake Coordinator confirms with the Scheduler that qualified staff are available for every requested visit, including weekends and holidays. The result is recorded on the intake checklist. If the full schedule cannot be covered, the agency declines or defers acceptance and offers referral to another provider.

At intake and at each plan update, the RN Supervisor (for personal care clients) or the Administrator or designee (for homemaker/companion-only clients) identifies whether the client is daily-dependent or high-risk and marks the client file and the schedule.

For each daily-dependent client, the RN Supervisor or designee writes a coverage plan naming the primary caregiver, at least one trained backup caregiver, the family or emergency contact, and the steps if no backup can be found. The plan is kept in the client file and reviewed at each plan update.
The Scheduler builds schedules from the client's written service agreement or plan of care. Day, time and tasks are not changed without the client's agreement, and the change is documented.
The Scheduler keeps a current list of available backup caregivers and an on-call roster. The on-call number is given to every caregiver and every client in writing.

Caregivers must call the on-call line at [PHONE] as early as possible, and at least [2] hours before the visit when they can, if they will be late or absent. If a caregiver does not arrive or check in, the Scheduler contacts the caregiver and the client within [30] minutes of the scheduled start time.

The Scheduler tells the client or representative by phone as soon as a visit is expected to be late or missed. The notice states the reason, the expected arrival time or replacement, and the agency contact. If the client cannot be reached, the Scheduler tries the emergency contact and records every attempt.

The Scheduler assigns a backup aide for the visit as soon as the absence is known. If the client is daily-dependent or high-risk and no backup can arrive within a safe time, the Scheduler notifies the RN Supervisor at once. The RN Supervisor decides whether to send another caregiver, arrange family help, or take other steps. For any client who may be in immediate danger, the Scheduler or RN Supervisor asks for a welfare check by calling 911.
Backup caregivers may only perform tasks within their training and competency, and only the tasks on the client's plan.

The Scheduler documents every missed visit in the missed-visit log on the same day. The entry includes the client, scheduled time, reason, who was notified and when, the backup arranged, and whether the visit was made up.

The Scheduler notifies the RN Supervisor of every missed visit for a high-risk client, whether or not a backup is sent. The RN Supervisor reviews the client's condition, decides whether a call or visit is needed, and documents the review in the client record.
The Scheduler offers a make-up visit when appropriate and the client wants one. Visits are billed only for services actually delivered, and EVV and payroll records must match (see SVC-09).
If a client is left without needed care because of a missed visit, the Administrator is notified the same day. The Administrator decides whether the event must be handled as an incident under SAF-02.

For disasters and emergencies, the coverage plan follows the agency's Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan. When a threat is imminent, staff contact clients who need ongoing services, confirm whether each will evacuate or stay home, and apply the agency's procedures for clients who stay at home (see SAF-04 and SAF-05; Rule 59A-8.027(9)-(10)).

The Administrator reviews the missed-visit log monthly. The review covers the number of missed visits, causes, caregivers or clients with repeat events, and the availability of backups. Results go to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-04).

If missed visits show that the agency cannot reliably cover its client load, the Administrator stops accepting new clients until staffing is adequate and takes corrective action, including recruiting more backup staff.

responsibilities.duty: Makes sure staffing is adequate to deliver all agreed visits, decides whether to hold admissions, reviews the missed-visit log monthly, and responds to repeat problems.
Confirms coverage before acceptance, builds schedules, notifies clients, assigns backups, escalates to the RN Supervisor and keeps the missed-visit log.
Identifies daily-dependent and high-risk clients, writes or approves coverage plans, reviews missed visits for high-risk clients and directs follow-up.
Reports lateness or absence promptly, completes assigned visits, performs only tasks on the plan and within training, and documents any changes in the client's condition.
Does not accept clients until the Scheduler confirms coverage and documents the decision.

documentation: Intake coverage checklist
Written coverage plan for each daily-dependent client
Missed-visit log with client notification and backup details
RN Supervisor review notes for high-risk clients
Schedules and schedule-change records
On-call roster and backup caregiver list
Monthly missed-visit review and quality assurance minutes

policies.title: Electronic Visit Verification and Timekeeping
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; all caregivers, schedulers, payroll and billing staff
federal: 29 CFR 785.38 (travel time between job sites during the workday)
policies.purpose: To verify that each visit actually took place as scheduled, to meet federal and Florida Medicaid electronic visit verification (EVV) requirements, and to keep time records, payroll and billing consistent and ready for review by regulators and payers.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] uses electronic visit verification for every visit paid by Medicaid. Federal law requires EVV for Medicaid personal care services (since 1/1/2020) and home health care services (since 1/1/2023) (42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)). The agency captures the six required data elements at every EVV visit: the type of service performed, the recipient, the date of service, the location of service delivery, the individual providing the service, and the start and end times. Before beginning Medicaid services, the agency will confirm the specific EVV system and data requirements of each SMMC Long-Term Care plan and of the Agency for Persons with Disabilities (APD) for each program it serves, and will follow them. The agency also uses the same system, or an equivalent, to record time for private-pay clients so that time worked, visits delivered, payroll and billing match. No bill is submitted for a visit that is not supported by verified time. The agency will keep the capability to produce a certified report of services delivered by individual staff member for any period requested by AHCA, within 2 hours of a request (3 hours if the period requested is longer than one year). Fee schedules and billing codes for Medicaid services follow Rule 59G-4.002, F.A.C.

definitions.definition: An electronic system that verifies the six required data elements of a home care visit: service type, recipient, date, location, provider and start and end times.
A visit record that is missing data, outside the authorized schedule, or does not match another record, and that must be corrected or explained before billing.
A correction to an EVV record made by authorized staff after the visit, with a documented reason, the editor's name and the date, and supporting proof.
A report, signed by the Administrator or designee as true and accurate, listing visits delivered by a specific staff member over a stated period.
The EVV platform designated by the SMMC LTC plan or APD, which may differ from the agency's own timekeeping system.

procedures: Before the agency serves any Medicaid client, the Administrator contacts each SMMC LTC plan and APD to confirm the required EVV system, how to register with it, data and billing-submission requirements, and any training the payer requires. The results are recorded in the payer file. Florida EVV vendor and aggregator details are confirmed directly with each payer and not assumed.
The Administrator designates an EVV Coordinator ([EVV COORDINATOR NAME]) who sets up the system, enters authorized visits, and keeps credentials and access current.
The EVV Coordinator enters each Medicaid client's authorization, including service type, units and dates, so the system can compare visits with what is authorized.

During orientation (see PER-03), every caregiver is trained on how to clock in and out, what to do when the phone or internet is unavailable, how to record the service type, and that clocking in or out for someone else is prohibited and grounds for discipline.

The caregiver clocks in at the client's home at arrival and clocks out at departure, so that the system captures the location, the caregiver, the client, the date and the start and end times. The caregiver records the type of service performed.

If the system cannot capture a visit (for example, no signal or a device failure), the caregiver calls the EVV Coordinator or on-call line at [PHONE] during the visit and completes a manual time form signed by the caregiver. The client or representative signs when the client is able to do so.
The EVV Coordinator reviews exceptions daily on business days. Missing clock-ins, late arrivals, visits outside the authorized schedule and mismatched locations are investigated and corrected.

Every manual edit must have a documented reason, the name of the person making the edit, the date, and supporting information such as the caregiver's statement or a call log. No edit may add time the caregiver did not work.
Payroll Staff compare EVV records to timesheets and payroll weekly for each pay period. Differences are resolved and documented before payroll is finalized.

Travel time between clients during the workday and other compensable time are handled in accordance with PER-08 and 29 CFR 785.38. Payroll Staff confirm with the Administrator the rules for travel time before the first pay period.
Billing Staff submit claims only for visits with verified EVV records that match authorizations. Claims for visits with unresolved exceptions are held until corrected.
Billing Staff compare claims to EVV records and payroll before submission. A visit is never billed for more units than were delivered.

The Administrator keeps the capability to produce a certified report of services by staff member for any period AHCA requests. The EVV Coordinator and Billing Staff run a test report each quarter to confirm they can produce one within 2 hours (3 hours if the period exceeds one year).

When AHCA, a payer or an auditor asks for a report, the Administrator or designee logs the time of the request, runs the report, checks it against payroll and billing, signs the certification and delivers it within the required time. A copy and delivery proof are kept.
EVV records are retained as part of client and billing records under REC-01, and are available for survey and payer audit.

Suspected falsified time, shared logins, or billing for visits not made is reported to the Administrator immediately and handled under GOV-05 (corporate compliance, fraud and billing integrity). The Administrator reports and corrects overpayments as required by the payer.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms payer EVV requirements, oversees compliance, signs certified reports and handles suspected falsification.
