Maintains the system, enters authorizations, reviews exceptions, approves manual edits and tests report capability each quarter.
Clocks in and out accurately at the client's location, records the service type, calls the agency when the system fails and never clocks in or out for another person.
Reconciles EVV, timesheets and payroll each pay period and applies wage and hour rules.
Bills only verified visits that match authorizations and holds claims with unresolved exceptions.
Keeps schedules aligned with authorizations so visits match what the payer approved.

documentation: Payer EVV requirements file for each SMMC LTC plan and APD
EVV visit records with the six data elements
Exception reports and manual edit log with reasons
Manual time forms for system failures
Payroll to EVV reconciliation records
Billing to EVV reconciliation records
Certified reports of services and request and delivery log
Quarterly report-capability test results
EVV training records for caregivers

policies.title: Change in Client Condition and Emergencies in the Home
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; all aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, RN supervisors and on-call staff
policies.purpose: To make sure caregivers recognize and report changes in a client's condition promptly, respond to emergencies in the home safely and within their scope, and notify the right people in the right order.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every caregiver to report observed changes in a client's condition or behavior and every emergency without delay. Aide training includes recognition of emergencies and follow-up appropriate to the aide's scope (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)7). Aides report observed changes in a client's condition to the RN supervisor, who decides whether to notify the client's physician. Homemakers and companions report unusual incidents or changes in behavior to the case manager and supervisor (Rule 59A-8.0095(12)). Aides and CNAs must hold current CPR certification (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(k)). In an emergency the caregiver calls 911 first, then the RN supervisor, then the family or emergency contact. Caregivers do not diagnose, give medical advice or perform tasks outside their training. Before any emergency occurs, the agency checks whether the client has a valid Do-Not-Resuscitate order so that staff know what to present to emergency responders.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening sign, symptom, behavior, function, mood, appetite, skin condition, mobility, or home situation that differs from the client's usual state, such as a fall, new confusion, shortness of breath, a pressure sore, or refusal of food or care.

A situation that presents an immediate threat to life, health or safety, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, trouble breathing, a stroke sign, serious injury, severe bleeding, a fire or an intruder.
An event, including an unexpected behavior, that is outside the client's normal pattern or the agency's expected care routine and that may affect the client's well-being.

A Florida Do-Not-Resuscitate Order on the form required by the state that is signed by the physician and the client or representative, and which is available in the home for emergency responders. See CR-08.
The person the client has named to be called in an emergency, recorded in the client record.

procedures: At intake, the RN Supervisor or Intake Coordinator records each client's emergency contact, physician, preferred hospital, allergies, medication list, and whether a valid DNR is in the home. The location of the DNR form is noted in the client file. See SVC-02 and CR-08.

During orientation, every caregiver is trained to recognize emergencies and changes in condition, to call 911, and to report to the supervisor. The caregiver demonstrates current CPR certification before working alone, and certification is kept current. See PER-03.
In an emergency, the caregiver first calls 911 and gives the address, the client's condition, and what has been done. The caregiver does not wait to reach a supervisor before calling 911.

While waiting for help, the caregiver stays with the client and provides only first aid and CPR within the caregiver's training and current certification, unless a valid DNR is presented. The caregiver follows 911 dispatcher instructions.

If a valid DNR order is in the home, the caregiver gives it to emergency responders. A caregiver who is unsure whether a DNR is valid calls 911 and follows dispatcher and responder direction, and then notifies the RN Supervisor. The agency does not delay emergency care to look for paperwork.

As soon as the caregiver can safely do so, the caregiver calls the RN Supervisor or on-call RN at [PHONE], then the family or emergency contact, and gives the facts: what happened, the client's condition, and where the client is being taken.

The caregiver does not leave the client alone while the emergency continues. If the client is transported, the caregiver provides the medication list and agency contact to the responders. The caregiver notifies the Scheduler so that other scheduled visits can be covered.

For a non-emergency change in condition, an aide reports to the RN Supervisor the same day, and by phone right away if the change is significant. Examples are a fall without injury, new confusion, decreased intake, a new skin change, swelling, a missed medication, or a refusal of care.

The RN Supervisor assesses the report by phone or visit as needed, decides whether to notify the physician, family or other provider, and decides whether the plan of care or task list needs to change. The RN Supervisor documents the report, the decision and who was notified.

Homemakers and companions report unusual incidents or changes in behavior to their supervisor, and to the client's case manager when the client has one, the same day. The supervisor decides whether an RN assessment or referral is needed and documents the follow-up.

Caregivers record the change or emergency in the client's service notes before the end of the shift, using objective facts: date, time, what was seen or heard, actions taken, who was called and the response.

If the event involves a fall, injury, death, abuse, neglect, exploitation, property loss or any other reportable event, the caregiver also completes an incident report within 24 hours and the Administrator handles it under SAF-02. Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported under SAF-01 immediately.
If the emergency is caused by a disaster, fire, severe weather or loss of power, the caregiver follows SAF-04 and SAF-05 and the client's disaster plan.

The RN Supervisor or Administrator follows up with the client or family within [24] hours after any emergency or hospital transport, updates the plan of care if needed (SVC-03), and decides whether services will continue, be held, or be changed.
The Administrator reviews emergencies and significant changes in condition each month and reports trends to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Recognizes and reports changes in condition, calls 911 first in an emergency, provides first aid and CPR within training, keeps CPR certification current and documents the event.
Reports unusual incidents or changes in behavior to the supervisor and case manager, calls 911 in an emergency, and does not perform hands-on care.
Receives reports, assesses, notifies the physician when needed, updates the plan of care, and documents decisions and follow-up.
Answer caregiver calls at all service hours, reach the RN Supervisor and family, and arrange coverage for affected visits.
Makes sure training and CPR are current, reviews incident reports and trends and makes sure reportable events are reported.

documentation: Emergency contact, physician and DNR status in the client record
Service notes describing the change or emergency
RN Supervisor notes of reports received, assessment, physician or family notification and decisions
Incident report (SAF-02) when required
CPR certification records in the personnel file
Orientation and competency records showing emergency recognition training
Monthly emergency and change-in-condition review

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; Administrator, RN supervisors, intake and records staff
policies.purpose: To make sure services end in an orderly, documented and safe way, that clients who need continuing care are referred to another provider before services stop, and that records are transferred and completed as required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not end services to a client who needs continuing care without first developing a plan and referring the client to another home health agency or appropriate provider. The client or representative receives written notice of the termination date, the reason, and the continuing-care plan (Rule 59A-8.020(4)). The requirement for a continuing-care plan and referral does not apply to private-pay clients who default on payment. Even so, when a client's private funds are depleted, the agency will help the client assess eligibility for government programs. Registered homemaker and companion providers keep a copy of any written termination notice in the client record (Rule 59A-8.025(8)(h)). When a client asks to transfer to another agency, the agency sends a copy of the record on request (Rule 59A-8.022(3)). A termination summary is completed for every client whose services end (Rule 59A-8.022(5)(l)).

definitions.definition: The end of services because the client's goals have been met, the client no longer needs the services, the client moves, or the client dies.
Movement of the client to another provider, agency or care setting, which may or may not be requested by the client.
The agency's decision to end services, or the client's decision to stop services, for any reason.
A written plan describing the client's ongoing needs, the provider or program the client is referred to, and the steps taken to avoid a gap in care.
Failure by a client who pays privately to pay for services after reasonable notice and an opportunity to cure.
A written record of the first and last visit dates, reason for termination, condition at discharge and disposition.

procedures: Only the Administrator or the Administrator's designee may approve termination or discharge of a client. The decision and its reason are recorded in the client record. Caregivers never end services on their own.

Termination for a reason other than the client's request or death may be considered only for these reasons: the home is no longer safe for staff or the client, the client no longer needs the agency's services, the agency can no longer safely meet the client's needs or provide all assigned visits, the client or payer does not pay, or the client repeatedly refuses the agreed services. The agency does not terminate because of a client's age, disability, race, sex, national origin, language or diagnosis (see CR-05).

Before ending services for a client who needs continuing care, the RN Supervisor (or the Administrator for homemaker and companion clients) develops a written continuing-care plan. The plan names the client's needs and the proposed receiving provider or program.

The Intake Coordinator or RN Supervisor refers the client to another home health agency or appropriate provider before services stop. The referral is by phone or in writing to at least [two] providers when available. Each referral, contact name, date and response is documented.

At the same time, the Administrator gives the client or representative written notice of the termination date, the reason for termination and the continuing-care plan. The notice is delivered by hand with a signature, or by mail with a copy kept, at least [14] days before the termination date unless immediate termination is needed for safety. Services continue until the notice period ends unless there is an imminent threat to staff or client safety.

If a private-pay client has defaulted on payment, the plan and referral steps above are not required. The Administrator still gives written notice with the date and reason, offers help in assessing eligibility for government programs when private funds are depleted, and tells the client what resources exist. This help includes referral to the Aging and Disability Resource Center or Area Agency on Aging and the Department of Children and Families, and the offer is documented.

The RN Supervisor or Administrator discusses the planned termination with the client or representative and with the family when appropriate, and answers questions. The client's wishes are documented. The agency tells the client how to file a complaint (see CR-02 and CR-07).

If a client's physician or case manager is involved, or the client receives Medicaid, the Administrator notifies them of the planned termination and works with the payer or plan so that care coordination continues (see SVC-12).

If the client or representative requests termination, the Administrator confirms the request in writing, or documents the verbal request, and asks the client to sign an acknowledgement. The RN Supervisor offers a continuing-care plan and referral if the client needs ongoing care.
If a client dies, is hospitalized for an extended stay, or moves out of the service area, the Administrator or designee documents the date and circumstances and closes the record.

If a client or representative asks to transfer to another agency, Records Staff send a copy of the clinical record to the new agency promptly after receiving a written request or authorization, and note the date, recipient and contents sent. Disclosure to anyone else requires written consent (see REC-04 and CR-03).
For registered homemaker and companion providers, a copy of any written termination notice is placed in the confidential client record.

Within [7] days after the last visit, the RN Supervisor (or the Administrator for homemaker and companion clients) completes the termination summary: first and last visit dates, reason for termination, the client's condition at discharge, and disposition, including where the client went and who was notified.

Records Staff close the record, confirm that all service notes and the signed agreement are present, and keep the record for the required retention period. The service provision plan for aide, homemaker and companion clients without a treatment order is kept for one year after termination (see REC-01).
The Administrator reviews all terminations each quarter and reports reasons and trends to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves all terminations, signs and issues written notices, makes sure referrals and continuing-care plans are done, and reviews terminations quarterly.
Writes the continuing-care plan for personal care clients, coordinates referral, completes the termination summary and communicates with the physician or case manager.
Contacts receiving providers, documents referrals and helps clients with eligibility information for government programs.
Send records on request to the new agency with required consent, close the record and confirm contents.
Report client statements about ending services to the supervisor and continue care until the effective date.

documentation: Documented reason and approval for termination
Continuing-care plan and referral record
Written termination notice with date, reason and plan, and proof of delivery
Client acknowledgement of a client-requested termination
Record of eligibility-assistance offer for clients whose private funds are depleted
Record transfer request, consent and log of what was sent
Termination summary
Quarterly termination review

policies.title: Coordination with Medicaid Programs and Payers
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; administrator, intake, scheduling, billing and compliance staff serving Medicaid and public-program clients
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] meets enrollment, authorization, staffing, training and billing requirements of Medicaid managed care plans, the Agency for Persons with Disabilities (APD) and other public payers, and respects clients' rights in home and community-based settings.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] serves Medicaid and public-program clients only after it has met the payer's enrollment and credentialing requirements. Network providers serving Statewide Medicaid Managed Care (SMMC) plans must be screened and enrolled with Florida Medicaid (42 CFR 438.602). Medicaid long-term care (LTC) clients are served through SMMC LTC plans (Aetna, Florida Community Care, Humana, Molina, Simply, Sunshine and United as of 9/30/2026). Plans negotiate rates with providers and there is no public rate schedule, so the agency confirms rates in writing in each contract. State-plan personal care (S9122) covers recipients under 21 only (Rule 59G-4.215), and the agency does not assume that it covers adult clients. APD iBudget Personal Supports staff must be 18 or older with a high school diploma or GED and 1 year of verifiable experience (or 30 college semester hours), and the agency keeps training records for 5 years as required by the iBudget Waiver Coverage and Limitations Handbook. Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) contract vendors for the Community Care for the Elderly (CCE), Home Care for the Elderly (HCE), Alzheimer's Disease Initiative (ADI) and Older Americans Act (OAA) programs, and review licensure, insurance, complaints and Clearinghouse results. The agency follows each payer's authorization, units and EVV requirements and does not bill clients for services the plan covers.

definitions.definition: A Statewide Medicaid Managed Care Long-Term Care plan that contracts with the state to authorize and pay for covered home and community-based services, including personal care, homemaker, companion and respite services, for enrolled members.
A provider that contracts with a managed care plan to deliver services to its members.
The plan's or payer's written approval of the type, amount (units), frequency and duration of a service for a specific client.
Services under the APD iBudget Florida waiver that help a client with daily living tasks, delivered by qualified Personal Supports staff.
The plan, APD waiver support coordinator or AAA case manager responsible for the client's care plan and for approving changes in services.
Federal standards in 42 CFR 441.301(c) (and 441.710 where applicable) for home and community-based services, including respect for client choice, privacy, dignity and community integration.

procedures: Before pursuing Medicaid or public-program work, the Administrator confirms that the agency has the required license or registration and meets the payer's standards for insurance, background screening and training. These are recorded in the payer file. See GOV-02 and GOV-08.

The Administrator completes Florida Medicaid provider screening and enrollment for the agency before serving any SMMC network plan member, and records the Medicaid provider ID and dates. Providers do not serve plan members until enrollment is complete.

The Administrator applies to be a network provider with each SMMC LTC plan the agency chooses to serve and keeps each signed contract. The contract file records negotiated rates, billing codes, authorization rules, EVV requirements, reporting duties and any training required by the plan.

The Administrator enrolls the agency as a provider with APD before serving iBudget clients and records the services approved, such as Personal Supports, respite or companion. The agency uses the rates and billing instructions published by APD.

For AAA-funded programs (CCE, HCE, ADI and OAA), the Administrator responds to vendor procurement and monitoring requests and provides the licensure, insurance, complaint history and Clearinghouse results the AAA requests.

The Intake Coordinator verifies each client's eligibility and the payer's authorization before the first visit. The authorization (service, units, dates and rate) is copied to the client record. Services are not started or extended beyond the authorization without the care coordinator's written approval.

The Intake Coordinator confirms with the plan or case manager who the client's care coordinator is and records the contact information. The RN Supervisor provides the plan of care and reports changes in the client's condition to the care coordinator in accordance with plan requirements. See SVC-03 and SVC-10.

The Scheduler staffs each Medicaid client within the authorized hours and tasks. Visits are not scheduled for more units or tasks than are authorized. If the client needs more care than was authorized, the RN Supervisor or Intake Coordinator asks the care coordinator to approve changes and documents the request.

For APD iBudget Personal Supports, the Administrator makes sure each staff member assigned is at least 18, has a high school diploma or GED, and has one year of verifiable experience or 30 college semester hours. This is verified before the person is assigned and kept in the personnel file. See PER-01 and PER-07.
Training records for APD iBudget staff, including completion of the training the handbook requires, are kept for 5 years. The Administrator reviews them annually. See PER-03.

The agency complies with each payer's EVV requirements (see SVC-09) and submits claims only for verified, authorized visits, at the contracted rate and billing code, in accordance with Rule 59G-4.002, F.A.C. for Medicaid schedules and codes.

The agency does not bill a client or family for any service covered by the plan or waiver, except for patient responsibility or share-of-cost amounts the payer identifies. Billing Staff report to the Administrator any client or family who is asked to pay for a covered service.

The agency delivers services in ways consistent with HCBS settings requirements. Staff respect the client's choices, privacy, dignity and right to receive visitors, and do not restrict the client's freedom in the home. See CR-01. Any restriction must be supported by the person-centered plan approved by the payer.

The Administrator checks managed care and APD provider notices at least [monthly] for changes in rates, authorization rules and billing instructions, and updates procedures and staff training. The Administrator keeps a record of notices received and actions taken.

If a client loses Medicaid eligibility, the Intake Coordinator tells the client and care coordinator immediately, gives the client written notice as required by SVC-11, and helps the client assess other eligibility options such as the DCF eligibility process and the Aging and Disability Resource Center or AAA.

Billing and compliance staff audit a sample of Medicaid claims each [month] against authorizations, EVV and payroll. Findings and any repayments are reported to the Administrator and handled under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Completes enrollment, contracts and credentialing, confirms rates and requirements, monitors payer notices and makes sure the agency meets each payer's standards.
Verifies eligibility and authorization, records the care coordinator and requests changes in services when needs change.
Schedules only authorized hours and tasks and monitors authorization limits.
Bills according to the contract, authorization and EVV, does not bill clients for covered services and audits claims.
Coordinates the plan of care with the care coordinator and reports changes in condition.
Verify and file iBudget Personal Supports qualifications and keep training records for 5 years.

documentation: Medicaid provider enrollment and screening records
Signed SMMC LTC plan and APD provider agreements, including negotiated rates
Payer authorizations (service, units, dates, rate) for each client
Care coordinator contact information and communication log
Records of AAA vendor reviews and submissions
iBudget Personal Supports staff qualification and training records (kept 5 years)
Payer notice log and procedure updates
Claim audit results and corrective actions

policies.title: Clients with Alzheimer's Disease or Related Disorders
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled services) license; Homemaker and Companion Services registration; all staff who have client contact, RN supervisors, intake and marketing staff
policies.purpose: To make sure clients with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders receive safe, appropriate care from trained staff, to prevent misleading claims about specialized dementia care, and to track required dementia training.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will make sure staff who serve clients with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders complete the dementia-related training required by s. 430.5025, F.S., as required by s. 400.4785, F.S. An HHA that claims to provide special care for persons with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders must disclose the services that make it suitable for such clients (s. 400.4785(2)). Unless the agency has developed and can document such special services, it will not advertise or claim special Alzheimer's care. Staff must complete the training in s. 430.5025: basic information about dementia at hire; a 1-hour course within 30 days for staff with client contact; and 2 additional hours within 7 months for HHA, nurse registry and homemaker/companion staff. Completion is tracked in each personnel file. Intake and the RN task list address wandering, behavior and elopement risk for every client with a dementia diagnosis or suspected cognitive impairment.

definitions.definition: Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, including vascular, Lewy body and frontotemporal dementia, that cause memory loss, confusion, behavior change and loss of function.

Any statement in advertising, marketing materials, the website, brochures or discussions that the agency provides specialized, dedicated or enhanced care for people with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders.
A client with cognitive impairment leaving the home or a safe area without supervision or without staff or family knowing, in a way that places the client at risk.
The training required by s. 430.5025, F.S., completed by staff according to the schedule in this policy.

procedures: The Administrator decides, in writing, whether [AGENCY NAME] will claim special care for clients with Alzheimer's disease or related disorders. The decision is reviewed at least annually and whenever services or marketing change.

If the agency does not claim special care, the Administrator does not permit any advertising, website, brochure or staff statement that says or implies the agency provides special Alzheimer's or dementia care. The Administrator reviews marketing materials before use, in accordance with GOV-02.

If the agency does claim special care, the Administrator prepares a written disclosure of the services that make the agency suitable for such clients, such as dementia-specific staff training beyond the minimum, care approaches, supervision and safety measures. The disclosure is given to clients and representatives before services begin and is available on request, in accordance with s. 400.4785(2).

At hire, Personnel Staff give each new employee with or without client contact basic information about dementia and record the date. The employee then completes the 1-hour dementia course within 30 days of hire if the employee has client contact.

Within 7 months of hire, homemaker, companion, aide and CNA staff complete 2 additional hours of dementia training, in addition to the 1-hour course. The training must meet s. 430.5025, F.S., and the Administrator keeps the provider's certificate or class record.

Personnel Staff keep a dementia training tracker listing each employee, hire date, 30-day deadline, 7-month deadline, completion dates, course provider and hours. The tracker is reviewed monthly. Staff who are approaching a deadline are reminded in writing 10 days ahead.

An employee who has not completed the 1-hour course by day 30 is not assigned to a client with dementia without a documented plan and supervision approved by the Administrator, and the course is completed at once. See PER-05.

At intake, the Intake Coordinator and RN Supervisor ask whether the client has a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or related disorder or shows signs of memory loss, confusion, wandering or behavior change, and record the answer. See SVC-02.

The RN Supervisor includes wandering, behavior and elopement risk in the assessment. The RN Supervisor records known triggers, past episodes of leaving the home, exit risks in the home (doors, gates, stairs), and whether the client needs a stand-by caregiver or supervision.

The RN task list for each client with dementia includes safety steps such as keeping doors secured as the family directs, never leaving the client unsupervised if the client is at risk, redirecting calmly, using a consistent routine, and contacting the family if the client cannot be found. The task list is reviewed with the caregiver before the first visit.
If a client with dementia cannot be found, the caregiver calls 911 immediately, then the RN Supervisor and the family. The agency documents the event and handles it under SAF-02. See SVC-10.

Caregivers use communication and care approaches taught in training: treat the client with respect, give simple choices and explanations, avoid arguing or restraining, and report new behavior, agitation or signs of pain to the RN Supervisor the same day.

The RN Supervisor reviews the plan of care and the caregiver's observations at each supervisory visit and updates the task list and risk assessment when the client's behavior or abilities change. See SVC-03 and SVC-04.
The Administrator reviews dementia training completion each quarter and reports any late training, caregiver concerns or elopement events to the quality assurance committee (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the agency will claim special Alzheimer's care, approves marketing, makes sure any required disclosure is made and makes sure training deadlines are met.
Track and file dementia training, send reminders and notify the Administrator of overdue training.
Assesses wandering, behavior and elopement risk, writes the task list, reviews with caregivers and updates the plan.
Asks about dementia diagnosis and symptoms at intake and records answers.
Completes required dementia training on time, follows the task list and reports behavior changes or missing client events right away.
Make no special Alzheimer's care claims unless approved by the Administrator.

documentation: Written decision on whether the agency claims special Alzheimer's care
Disclosure of special services, if the agency makes such a claim, and proof it was provided to clients
Dementia training tracker
Training certificates and class records in each personnel file
Intake and assessment entries on dementia, wandering, behavior and elopement risk
RN task list for clients with dementia
Incident reports for elopement or missing-client events
Quarterly training review

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Mandatory Reporting
policies.applies_to: All owners, administrators, alternate administrators, RN supervisors, home health aides/CNAs, homemakers, companions, office staff, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME], under the Home Health Agency (non-skilled) license, the Homemaker and Companion Services registration, or the Nurse Registry track, as applicable.
policies.purpose: To protect clients from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure every suspected case is reported immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline and handled without delay, retaliation or private investigation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, or exploitation of any client, whether by staff, family, other caregivers or third parties. Every person who works for or on behalf of [AGENCY NAME] who knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that a vulnerable adult has been, or is being, abused, neglected or exploited must report it immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline operated by the Department of Children and Families (DCF) at 1-800-962-2873. This duty belongs to each individual and cannot be delegated to, or delayed for, a supervisor or the administrator. Staff must also report a suspected death caused by abuse. Staff must not investigate, confront the suspected abuser, or wait for approval before reporting. After reporting, staff notify the administrator or alternate administrator. The agency gives each client the abuse hotline notice on or before the first day of service (s. 408.810(5)), as described in CR-07, and screens, trains and supervises staff to prevent abuse.

definitions.definition: A person 18 or older whose ability to perform normal activities of daily living or to provide for his or her own care or protection is impaired because of a mental, emotional, physical or developmental disability or dysfunction, or brain damage, or the infirmities of aging.

Any willful act or threatened act that causes or is likely to cause significant impairment to a client's physical, mental or emotional health, including hitting, slapping, harassment, intimidation, isolation, sexual contact, or improper restraint.

Failure or omission by a caregiver to provide the care, supervision and services necessary to maintain the client's physical and mental health, including food, clothing, medicine, shelter and health care, or failure to make a reasonable effort to protect the client from abuse, neglect or exploitation by others.
Improper use of a client's funds, property or assets, by deception, intimidation or other means, for the benefit of someone other than the client.
A good-faith concern based on what a staff member sees, hears, or is told. Proof is not required before reporting.

procedures: Before a new hire works with any client, the administrator confirms that level 2 background screening is complete and cleared under PER-02. Any person with a disqualifying offense is not permitted to work with clients.

At hire and before client contact, each staff member completes training on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation. The training covers physical, emotional and financial warning signs, the hotline number, and this policy. The staff member signs an acknowledgement kept in the personnel file (PER-07).
Each staff member repeats the training at least annually as part of in-service (PER-03). The administrator records the date, content and attendance.

A staff member who witnesses or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation first ensures the client's immediate safety. If anyone is in immediate danger or needs emergency care, the staff member calls 911.

The staff member then immediately calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 and gives the client's name and address, the nature of the concern, the suspected person if known, and any other facts. The report is not delayed to get approval from a supervisor or the administrator.
If a staff member suspects that a client's death was caused by abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member reports that suspicion to the hotline immediately.

The staff member writes down the hotline intake or reference number and the date and time of the call, then notifies the administrator or alternate administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME], [PHONE]) as soon as possible, and the same day in all cases.
Staff do not investigate, interview the client about the allegation, confront the suspected abuser, destroy or alter evidence, or promise the client or family that the matter will be kept secret.
The administrator confirms that a hotline report was made. If the report cannot be confirmed, the administrator makes it personally and immediately.

The administrator removes any staff member who is the subject of an allegation from contact with the client, or puts other protections in place, while the matter is reviewed. The administrator cooperates fully with DCF, law enforcement and AHCA.

The administrator records the event in the incident log under SAF-02 within 24 hours, with the hotline intake number, actions taken, and outcome. The record is kept apart from the client's clinical record with restricted access.
The RN supervisor, or the administrator if there is no RN, updates the client's plan of care and assigned caregivers as needed to keep the client safe (SVC-03).
The agency prohibits retaliation against any person who reports in good faith. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination (PER-09).

On or before the first day of service, the agency gives each client the abuse hotline notice, along with the complaint and Medicaid fraud hotline notices, in the approved statutory wording, and obtains a signed receipt as described in CR-07. The notice is also posted in the office.
The administrator reviews reports and trends at least quarterly in the quality review (GOV-04) and corrects staffing, training or supervision problems found.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect, exploitation or abuse-related death to the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately, notify the administrator after reporting, and never investigate or confront.
Confirm hotline reports were made, protect the client, remove or restrict the accused staff member as needed, cooperate with investigators, and document the event.
Watch for warning signs during supervisory visits, report suspicions to the hotline, and update the plan of care to protect the client.
Make sure screening, training, posting and client notice requirements are met and that no retaliation occurs.

documentation: Hotline report details, including intake number, date and time (restricted file)
Incident log entry (SAF-02)
Staff training and annual in-service rosters on abuse reporting
Signed staff acknowledgements of this policy
Level 2 screening results (PER-02)
Signed client receipt of abuse hotline notice (CR-07)
Corrective action and administrator follow-up notes

policies.title: Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] staff and contractors providing or supervising client services under the Home Health Agency (non-skilled), Homemaker and Companion registration, or Nurse Registry track.
policies.purpose: To make sure incidents involving clients or staff are reported internally, investigated promptly, tracked for trends, and reported externally when required.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps an internal incident log and investigates every incident within a set time. Chapter 59A-8, F.A.C., does not require home health agencies to file a general adverse-incident report with AHCA, so this policy does not create one. It does require immediate reporting of suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the Florida Abuse Hotline (1-800-962-2873, see SAF-01), reporting to AHCA within 21 calendar days of changes in application information (s. 408.810(3)), and any payer or plan notifications required by contract. Incident data are reviewed in the quality program (GOV-04).

definitions.definition: Any unplanned event that harms or could have harmed a client or staff member, or that involves loss of or damage to property, including falls, injuries, medication errors or refusals, property loss or damage, allegations of misconduct, vehicle accidents during client transport, emergency calls, and a client's death.
The agency's running record of every incident, with investigation and outcome.
An event that could have caused harm but did not. Near misses are logged for quality purposes.

procedures: Staff who are present at or discover an incident first make sure the client and others are safe and call 911 for any emergency (see SVC-10).
The staff member notifies the RN supervisor or administrator by phone immediately, and always before the end of the shift, using the contact numbers on the care plan ([PHONE]).

The staff member completes the written incident report form within 24 hours with the date, time, place, persons involved, what happened, what was observed, actions taken, and who was notified. The report states facts only.
The administrator or alternate administrator enters the incident into the incident log within one business day, assigns a log number, and designates an investigator.

Investigation begins within 24 hours of the report and is completed within 7 calendar days unless an outside agency asks the agency to wait. The investigator interviews those involved, reviews the plan of care and visit records, and identifies the cause.

If the incident involves a suspected case of abuse, neglect or exploitation, staff and the administrator follow SAF-01 and the hotline report is made immediately. The incident log records the hotline intake number.

For a client's death, the administrator notifies the client's representative as appropriate, notifies the payer or plan if the contract requires it, and records the circumstances. If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected as a cause, SAF-01 applies.
For a medication-related incident, the RN supervisor reviews the event under SVC-06, contacts the client's physician or pharmacist if needed, and retrains staff as appropriate.
The RN supervisor assesses any client who was injured or whose condition changed and updates the plan of care (SVC-03).
The administrator tells the client or representative about the incident and its outcome, in line with the agency's privacy policy (CR-03).

The administrator checks the notification needs for each incident: Abuse Hotline, payer/plan notices required by contract, workers' compensation and insurance carriers, and law enforcement where indicated.

If an event changes information in the license or registration application, such as ownership, administrator, insurance or similar facts, the administrator reports the change to AHCA within 21 calendar days (s. 408.810(3)) and records the date sent.
The administrator writes corrective actions on the log and sets due dates. Corrective actions may include staff retraining, supervision changes, or changes to the care plan or agency procedure.
Each quarter the administrator summarizes incident counts, types and trends and gives the summary to the quality review committee (GOV-04) and to the governing body.
Incident reports and the log are kept as confidential administrative records for the retention period in REC-01 and are available to AHCA surveyors (REC-04).

responsibilities.duty: Secure safety, call 911 if needed, notify the supervisor immediately, and submit a written report within 24 hours.
Assess affected clients, review clinical aspects, update the plan of care, and support the investigation.
Maintain the incident log, ensure investigation timelines, make external reports and notifications, and track corrective actions.
Review quarterly incident summaries and ensure corrective actions are completed.

documentation: Written incident report forms
Incident log with log numbers, investigation findings and corrective actions
Hotline intake numbers (restricted file)
Copies of any notifications to AHCA, payers, plans or insurers
Quarterly incident trend summaries (GOV-04)

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] aides, CNAs, homemakers, companions, RN supervisors and office staff who have contact with clients, client homes, or agency equipment.
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among clients and staff through training, standard precautions, correct use of protective equipment, and safe handling of waste and sharps.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows standard precautions in every client home and in the office. Under Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c), aide training includes basic infection control: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment (PPE), bag technique and equipment disinfection. Although Rule 59A-8.0095 gives responsibility for CDC- and OSHA-consistent infection control to the director of nursing in skilled agencies, and a non-skilled agency is not required to have a director of nursing, [AGENCY NAME] voluntarily adopts that standard. The administrator, with the RN supervisor, is responsible for this policy. The agency provides no skilled nursing, injections, wound care or other tasks that generate biomedical waste, and it states that it generates no biomedical waste. Staff do not handle clients' sharps except as set out below.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all clients regardless of diagnosis, including hand hygiene, PPE, safe handling of body fluids, respiratory hygiene, and cleaning of equipment.
Personal protective equipment such as gloves, gowns, masks and eye protection.
A method of carrying and using supplies in the home that keeps clean supplies and equipment from becoming contaminated.
Needles, lancets, syringes and other items that can puncture the skin.

procedures: The administrator and RN supervisor adopt written infection control procedures consistent with current CDC guidance and OSHA requirements and review them at least annually.

At orientation and before client contact, each aide completes infection control training covering hand hygiene, PPE, bag technique, equipment disinfection, and respiratory etiquette (PER-03, PER-04). The trainer documents attendance and competency.
Staff perform hand hygiene at the start and end of each visit, before and after glove use, before food preparation, and after toileting assistance or handling soiled items.

The agency supplies gloves, masks, gowns, eye protection, hand sanitizer and disinfectant wipes in the sizes staff need, at no cost to staff. Staff replace PPE that is torn, wet or soiled, and dispose of it in household trash in a sealed bag.
Staff use gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, broken skin, mucous membranes or soiled linens or items, and remove gloves before touching clean surfaces or leaving the room.
Staff carry supplies in a clean bag, place the bag on a clean surface, keep it away from pets and soiled areas, and disinfect reusable equipment after each use with an approved product.
Staff launder soiled linen separately in the client's washer when the client has one, following the client's plan, and dispose of heavily soiled disposable items in sealed bags.

Staff do not work when they have symptoms of a contagious illness such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, or a respiratory infection. They call the supervisor, who finds a replacement and follows PER-06 for return to work.
Staff who see signs of infection in a client, including fever, new cough, rash, wound redness, or diarrhea, report it to the RN supervisor the same day under SVC-10.

No biomedical waste is generated by this agency. If a staff member finds a client's loose sharps in the home, the staff member does not recap or pick up sharps with bare hands. The staff member tells the client or representative and the supervisor, and advises placing sharps in a rigid, puncture-resistant container such as a sturdy plastic detergent bottle, or a commercial sharps container.

If a staff member has a needlestick, sharps injury or exposure to blood or body fluids, the staff member washes the area immediately, calls the supervisor, seeks medical evaluation the same day, and completes an incident report (SAF-02). The agency pays for post-exposure evaluation as required by OSHA.
The administrator gives staff access to the bloodborne pathogen exposure control information that applies to their jobs and keeps training records for each employee.
The administrator reviews infection-related incidents and staff illness trends at least quarterly in the quality review (GOV-04).
During an outbreak or public health directive, the administrator follows guidance from the Florida Department of Health and notifies staff and clients of any changes in precautions.

responsibilities.duty: Adopt and review this policy, ensure supplies and training, and follow up on exposures and illness.
Train and check aide technique, assess client signs of infection, and advise on precautions.
Use standard precautions, wear PPE, stay home when ill, and report exposures and client infection signs.

documentation: Written infection control procedures with annual review dates
Infection control training and competency records (PER-03, PER-04)
Incident reports for exposures (SAF-02)
Employee illness and return-to-work records (PER-06)
PPE supply and distribution records

policies.title: Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP) and Client Disaster Plans
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] administrator, alternate administrator, designated emergency coordinator, RN supervisor and all staff who serve clients, under the Home Health Agency license (and the Nurse Registry track where AHCA requires a plan).
policies.purpose: To keep the agency able to protect clients and continue or reasonably coordinate services before, during and after hurricanes, floods, fires, power loss and other emergencies.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan (CEMP) in the format of AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. March 2013), as required by s. 400.492 and Rule 59A-8.027(1). The plan is forwarded electronically to the designated Department of Health (DOH) contact for approval (Rule 59A-8.027(2)). The agency reviews the CEMP annually and makes substantive changes as needed (Rule 59A-8.027(3)). The agency tells the county emergency management office and county health department about changes in coordinating staff phone numbers, including after-hours numbers, for each county on the license (Rule 59A-8.027(4)). Designated staff are briefed on their duties and a telephone-outage contingency is in place (Rule 59A-8.027(6)). When an emergency threatens, the agency contacts clients who need ongoing services (Rule 59A-8.027(9)).

definitions.definition: The agency's written Comprehensive Emergency Management Plan on AHCA Form 3110-1022.
The staff member responsible for carrying out the CEMP and being the contact for county emergency officials.
An emergency, such as a hurricane warning or evacuation order, that is about to affect the service area.

procedures: The administrator prepares the CEMP on AHCA Form 3110-1022 (rev. March 2013) covering every county in the agency's service area and names an emergency coordinator and a backup.
The administrator submits the CEMP electronically to the DOH-designated contact for approval and keeps the submission confirmation and the approval response.

At each license renewal, the administrator makes sure the CEMP has been approved or that proof of submission within the last 365 days is available for the renewal application, as AHCA's application requires.

The administrator reviews the CEMP at least once a year, before the start of hurricane season, and records the date. The review is repeated and the plan is revised after any activation, drill or change in service area.

When any coordinating staff phone number changes, including after-hours numbers, the administrator notifies the emergency management office and the health department of every county on the license and records the date and method of notice.
The administrator briefs designated staff on their CEMP duties at hire and at least annually, and keeps sign-in records.

The agency keeps a telephone-outage contingency. Options include staff cell phones, a ham radio operator, public service announcements, or driving to the client's home, and the plan names which will be used.
At each client's admission, staff discuss disaster planning with the client and caregiver and complete the evacuation or stay-at-home decision under SAF-05.

When an emergency is imminent, the emergency coordinator activates the CEMP, reviews the prioritized client list (SAF-05), and contacts clients who need ongoing services to confirm their plans, caregivers and supplies.
Staff call or visit clients in priority order, tell each client what the agency can and cannot do, confirm the client's plan, and record each contact and its result in the client record.

During and after the emergency, the emergency coordinator keeps contact with clients to the extent safe, confirms their status, and arranges services as conditions allow. Staff are told not to put themselves in danger.
If the agency has to stop operating, it notifies clients as required (GOV-09) and tells them where to get care.
After the emergency, the administrator holds a review within 30 days, records lessons learned, and updates the CEMP and the quality review (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Prepare, submit, review and update the CEMP, notify county offices of phone changes, and brief staff.
Activate the plan, contact clients, direct staff, and keep records of contacts.
Help identify high-need clients and advise on client needs during an emergency.
Know their duties, keep contact information current, and follow instructions during an emergency.

documentation: Current CEMP on AHCA Form 3110-1022
DOH submission confirmation and approval
Annual review record with date
Notices to county emergency management offices and county health departments
Staff briefing rosters
Client contact logs during emergencies
After-action review

policies.title: Special Needs Registry, Evacuation and Shelter-in-Place Planning
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] administrator, RN supervisor, intake staff, emergency coordinator and aides who serve clients under the Home Health Agency license (and the Nurse Registry track where applicable).
policies.purpose: To make sure every client and caregiver knows about the county special needs registry, has a documented evacuation or stay-home plan, and that the agency can prioritize clients when an emergency occurs.
policies.policy: On admission, [AGENCY NAME] informs each client and caregiver about the special needs registry kept by the county emergency management office (s. 252.355) and documents in the client file whether the client plans to evacuate or stay at home, whether the caregiver can take responsibility for services, or whether the agency must continue services (Rule 59A-8.027(8)). The agency collects registration information for special needs clients and submits it to the county emergency management office as required, and educates registered clients that special needs shelters are a last resort and that care there may not equal care received at home (Rule 59A-8.027(13)-(17)). The agency keeps a current prioritized client list, a client-specific list of medications, supplies and equipment in the home, and written procedures for clients who stay home. If the agency cannot continue services to a special needs client, it documents the efforts it made.

definitions.definition: A registry kept by the county emergency management office of persons who need assistance during an emergency, as provided in s. 252.355.
A county-designated shelter for people with medical or functional needs who cannot go to a general population shelter.
A list ranking clients by the urgency of their need for continued services in an emergency.
Staying at home during an emergency instead of evacuating.

procedures: At admission (SVC-02), the intake nurse or administrator tells the client and caregiver about the county special needs registry and gives written information on how to register for the county where the client lives.

The staff member completes the disaster planning section of the admission record and documents whether the client will evacuate or stay home, where the client will go, who will transport, and whether a caregiver can take responsibility for services or the agency must continue services.

For each client who wants to register or needs special needs registry help, the staff member collects the registration information and submits it to the county emergency management office, then records the date of submission.

Staff explain that special needs shelters are a last resort, that conditions and care may not equal those at home, and that clients should bring medications, supplies, equipment, identification and a caregiver when possible. Staff note in the record that this education was provided.

The RN supervisor ranks each client by need for continued services (for example, dependence on equipment that needs power, inability to move without help, no caregiver, or dementia) and the emergency coordinator keeps the prioritized client list.

Staff make a client-specific list of the medications, supplies and equipment in the home, with the help of the client and caregiver and in line with the plan of care, and update it whenever the plan changes (SVC-03).

The agency keeps written procedures for clients who plan to stay at home. They include checking on the client before the storm if safe, helping the client stock food, water and medication, confirming caregiver availability, and giving emergency phone numbers.
The emergency coordinator reviews the prioritized client list and the evacuation and stay-home decisions at least every 6 months, and whenever a client's condition or living arrangements change.

When an imminent threat is announced, the emergency coordinator follows SAF-04 and contacts clients on the list in priority order, confirms their decisions, and reminds them of registry and shelter information.
If a client is ordered to evacuate and chooses to go to a special needs shelter, staff help confirm the registration and transportation arrangements and tell the family or caregiver.

If the agency cannot continue services to a special needs client, the emergency coordinator documents each effort made, including dates, times, persons contacted, and the outcome, and tells the client or representative what alternatives are available.
Staff do not take clients in their own vehicles during an evacuation unless the administrator has approved it under SAF-07.
The administrator reviews registry submissions, the prioritized list and activation records in the annual CEMP review (SAF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Educate the client at admission, document the evacuation or stay-home decision, and rank clients by need.
Keep the prioritized list, submit registry information to the county, and contact clients in an emergency.
Make sure planning is documented for every client and that records of efforts are kept.
Report changes in the client's condition, supplies or caregiver availability that affect the plan.

documentation: Admission record with registry education and evacuation or stay-home decision
Registry submission records
Prioritized client list with review dates
Client-specific medication, supply and equipment lists
Written procedures for clients who stay home
Emergency contact logs and records of efforts when services could not continue

policies.title: Caregiver Safety in the Home and Workplace Violence
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees and supervisors who work in client homes or the office. Independent contractors under the Nurse Registry track are covered as set out in the agency's contractor agreements.
policies.purpose: To protect caregivers from injury, violence and unsafe conditions, and to give staff clear authority to leave an unsafe situation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a workplace free of recognized hazards. Workers' compensation coverage is mandatory for a non-construction employer with four or more employees, and part-time employees count toward that number (s. 440.02); the agency carries that coverage once it meets the threshold and as a matter of policy for all employees. Aide training covers maintaining a clean and safe environment and safe transfer techniques with appropriate equipment (Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c)). The agency has procedures for unsafe homes, firearms, aggressive clients or family, pets, smoking and after-hours reporting. Any staff member may leave an unsafe situation and call the supervisor, without penalty.

definitions.definition: A condition in or around the home that threatens the staff member's health or safety, such as threats or violence, weapons displayed or misused, intoxicated persons, hazardous conditions, infestations, or aggressive animals.
Any threat, harassment, intimidation or physical violence directed at a staff member, whether from a client, family member, visitor or coworker, in a client home or the office.
The supervisor or administrator on call outside regular office hours, reached at [PHONE].

procedures: The administrator confirms workers' compensation coverage is in force when the agency has four or more employees, counting part-time staff. The administrator keeps the policy declarations page and posts the required workers' compensation notice.

At hire and annually, each staff member is trained on safe work practices, body mechanics, safe transfer techniques with appropriate equipment, and keeping a clean and safe environment (PER-03, PER-04). The trainer records attendance.

At intake (SVC-02), the RN or administrator completes a home safety review that asks about firearms, aggressive family members or animals, smoking, oxygen, clutter and hazards, lighting, stairs, utilities, and pests. The results go into the client record and the care plan.

Where there are firearms in the home, staff ask that they be stored unloaded and locked or out of sight during visits. Staff never handle a firearm. If the client or family refuses and the staff member feels unsafe, the staff member leaves and calls the supervisor.
Where there are pets, staff ask that animals be secured during the visit. A staff member who feels unsafe because of an animal does not have to enter the home.

Where a client or family member smokes, or oxygen is in use, staff follow the care plan and SVC-07. Staff do not light or hold a cigarette for a client and ask that smoking not occur near oxygen or during hands-on care.

A staff member who is threatened, harassed or assaulted, or who sees conditions that put them at risk, may leave immediately, go to a safe place, and call 911 if needed. The staff member then calls the supervisor or the after-hours contact at [PHONE]. No staff member will be disciplined for leaving an unsafe situation in good faith.

The supervisor decides what happens next, which may include a joint visit, a change of staffing, a change in the visit schedule, or notification to the client's physician, payer or law enforcement. The supervisor tells the client or family why services are being changed, following SVC-08 and SVC-11.

Staff on late or early shifts, or who work alone, check in with the office at the start and end of each visit. EVV (SVC-09) is used to confirm location, and the office follows up when a check-in is missed.
The staff member completes an incident report within 24 hours of any injury, threat or unsafe situation (SAF-02). The administrator investigates and records corrective action.
Injured employees report the injury to the supervisor immediately. The administrator files the first report of injury with the workers' compensation carrier and tells the employee where to get care.
Staff protect themselves from bloodborne pathogens and infections as set out in SAF-03, and the agency provides PPE at no cost.

Staff do not use or transport clients' belongings or work in homes where the condition of the dwelling prevents safe care. The RN supervisor assesses and discusses with the client or family and, if conditions cannot be fixed, follows SVC-11.
The administrator reviews injuries, threats and unsafe-home reports each quarter in the quality review (GOV-04) and corrects staffing, training or procedure gaps.
The agency does not retaliate against any staff member for reporting a safety concern.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain workers' compensation coverage, provide PPE and training, investigate incidents and make sure an after-hours contact is available.
Complete home safety reviews, respond to staff reports of unsafe conditions, and adjust the plan of care or staffing.
Follow safe work practices, report hazards, threats and injuries immediately, and leave an unsafe situation and call for help when necessary.
Support staff authority to leave unsafe situations and fund needed equipment and training.

documentation: Workers' compensation policy declarations page
Home safety review in each client record
Incident reports for injuries, threats and unsafe situations (SAF-02)
First reports of injury and carrier correspondence
Training records on safe transfers, body mechanics and workplace safety (PER-03)
Supervisor follow-up notes and corrective actions
Quarterly safety summaries (GOV-04)

policies.title: Transporting Clients
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled) staff, Homemaker and Companion registrant staff, and any contracted caregivers who may accompany or drive clients
policies.purpose: To set clear, safe and lawful rules for any time [AGENCY NAME] staff accompany or drive clients in a vehicle, and to protect clients, staff and the agency from avoidable injury and liability.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not provide transportation as a stand-alone service. Staff may accompany clients to doctors' appointments, outings and shopping when the service agreement and plan of care include it. Staff may drive a client in a vehicle only when the Administrator has authorized that employee in writing, the client (or representative) has given written consent, and the driver and vehicle meet the requirements below. Florida Chapter 59A-8 sets no specific client-transport standard, so this is an internal safety policy. The agency accepts a client only when services can be provided adequately and safely, and it supplies capable staff for all scheduled visits (Rule 59A-8.025, F.A.C.). Accompanying a client on an outing does not permit hands-on personal care by companion-only (registrant) staff.

definitions.definition: Going with a client to an appointment, shopping or an outing while the client is driven by someone else, uses public or paratransit transportation, or is transported by a medical transport provider.
Operating a motor vehicle with a client as a passenger as part of assigned work.
Liability coverage for the agency when employees use their own vehicles for agency business.
An employee approved in writing by the Administrator after the checks in this policy.

procedures: At intake (SVC-02), the intake coordinator asks whether the client needs or expects transportation or accompaniment and records the answer on the assessment.

If transportation is needed, the Administrator or RN Supervisor decides whether the agency can meet the need safely. The decision considers the client's mobility, cognition, behavior and equipment. If it cannot, the client is told before services start and is referred to other transportation resources.
Any transportation or accompaniment task must be written into the service agreement and the plan of care (CR-06, SVC-03), including who drives and which destinations are covered.

Before a client is driven, the client or representative signs the Client Transportation Consent form. It explains that staff use their own vehicle (or an agency vehicle), the driver's limits and the client's right to decline. The signed form is kept in the client record.

The Administrator authorizes a caregiver as a driver only after confirming a current valid driver license, current proof of auto insurance and a driving-record review. These are documented in the personnel file (PER-07).

The Administrator confirms in writing with the agency's insurance carrier or broker that liability and non-owned auto coverage apply to employees driving clients. The agency also confirms its liability insurance meets the minimum required for its license or registration type. The confirmation is renewed at each policy renewal and kept in the governance files.
If the insurer does not confirm coverage, no staff member may drive clients until coverage is in place. Staff may still accompany clients who travel by another means.

Authorized drivers must wear a seatbelt and ensure the client is buckled before the vehicle moves. Children, pets and non-client passengers are not allowed unless the Administrator approves it in advance.

Wheelchair users may be driven only in a vehicle designed for it, with securement equipment, and only by a caregiver trained in its use. Staff do not lift a client bodily into a vehicle. Transfers are limited to those in the plan of care and within the aide's training (SVC-01, SVC-04).

Drivers must not use a handheld phone, drive while impaired or fatigued, or drive when the client's behavior makes driving unsafe. If a client becomes agitated or unsafe, the driver stops in a safe place, calls the on-duty supervisor and, if necessary, 911.
Staff must not leave a client unattended in a vehicle, and must stay with the client at the destination as directed by the plan of care.
Staff must not use the client's vehicle unless the Administrator has approved it in writing and the client has consented. Staff must not accept payment or gifts for transportation (CR-04).
The driver completes a Transportation Log each trip showing date, times, start and end locations and any incident. The log is submitted to the supervisor with the visit record.
A crash, injury, fall during transfer, or client behavioral event is reported to the supervisor immediately and handled under SAF-02 and SAF-01 where applicable. Emergencies follow SVC-10.
The Administrator reviews transport logs and incidents quarterly as part of Quality Assurance (GOV-04) and may suspend a staff member's driving authorization at any time.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the agency offers driving, authorizes drivers, confirms insurance coverage in writing and reviews logs and incidents.
Assesses client mobility and safety for transport, trains staff on securement and transfer limits, and responds to transport incidents.
Follows this policy, keeps license and insurance current, reports changes at once and completes the log.
Identifies transportation needs at intake and ensures consent is obtained before driving.

documentation: Client Transportation Consent form (client record)
Service agreement and plan of care entries listing transportation tasks
Driver authorization, license, insurance proof and driving-record review (personnel file)
Insurance carrier written confirmation of coverage
Transportation Log and incident reports

policies.title: Caregiver Qualifications and CNA/Home Health Aide Certification Verification
policies.applies_to: Home Health Agency (non-skilled) hiring of home health aides and CNAs; Homemaker and Companion registrant hiring of companions and homemakers; contracted caregivers under any nurse registry arrangement; staff serving APD iBudget Personal Supports clients
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who gives hands-on care for [AGENCY NAME] meets Florida's minimum qualifications, and that proof is on file before the first client visit.
policies.policy: No person may provide hands-on personal care until the personnel file shows the credential or training required by Rule 59A-8.0095, F.A.C. A certified nursing assistant (CNA) must have current Florida certification, or a copy of another state's current certificate on file. Any other home health aide must have documented 40 hours of training or a passed competency test. Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses (Florida or another state) and nursing school graduates awaiting boards may work as aides under the rule. Staff who serve clients through the APD iBudget Personal Supports program must also meet the handbook qualifications. [AGENCY NAME] is not Medicare-certified, so Medicare Conditions of Participation aide training is not applied. Staff performing companion or homemaker work only do not provide hands-on personal care, and their duties are limited as described in SVC-01.

definitions.definition: A person who provides hands-on personal care and related tasks under RN supervision.
A certified nursing assistant holding a current certificate.
Checking the credential directly with the issuing registry or board, and printing or saving the result.
Staff who deliver APD iBudget Personal Supports and must be 18 or older, hold a high school diploma or GED, and have one year of verifiable experience (or 30 college semester hours).

procedures: The Administrator or designated hiring coordinator reviews each applicant's application and credentials before an offer is made. Offers are conditional until all required verification is complete.

For an applicant who claims to be a Florida CNA, the coordinator verifies on the Florida Board of Nursing / Department of Health license lookup that the certification is current and in good standing. A dated printout is placed in the personnel file.
For a CNA certified in another state, the coordinator obtains a copy of the current certificate, verifies it with the issuing state's registry when available, and files both.

For an applicant without CNA certification, the coordinator confirms either (a) documentation of a completed 40-hour training that meets Rule 59A-8.0095(5)(c), or (b) a passed competency test under PER-04. If neither exists, the applicant may not be scheduled for hands-on care until PER-04 is completed and passed.

For an RN or LPN applicant, the coordinator verifies license status in Florida or the other state. For a nursing school graduate awaiting boards, the coordinator obtains proof of graduation and files it. These persons are used as aides and supervised as aides.
For training taken at another agency or school, the RN Supervisor reviews the documentation and validates the aide's competency in person before assignment (PER-04).
If the aide will assist with medications, the file must also show the 2-hour medication assistance course with the label-reading check (PER-03, SVC-06).

For staff who will serve APD iBudget Personal Supports clients, the coordinator confirms age (18+), diploma or GED, and one year of verifiable experience (or 30 college semester hours), and files proof. Training records for these staff are kept for 5 years.

The coordinator completes the Caregiver Qualification Checklist and signs and dates it. The Administrator countersigns before the first assignment. The Level 2 screening and employment verification in PER-02 must also be complete.
The coordinator records each certificate's expiration date in the credential tracking log and reviews the log monthly.

At least 60 days before a certificate expires, the coordinator notifies the aide in writing of the renewal date. Proof of renewal must be filed before expiration. An aide whose certification has lapsed is removed from the schedule until it is renewed.

If a credential is found to be false, expired or revoked, the Administrator removes the person from client assignments immediately, reviews services already provided, and reports to the appropriate authority as needed (SAF-01, REC-02).
For companion/homemaker-only staff, the file shows a signed job description limited to non-hands-on duties, and the supervisor reviews that limit with the worker at hire.
The Administrator reviews a sample of personnel files quarterly under GOV-04 to confirm all items are present.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures no aide is assigned before qualifications are verified, and countersigns the checklist.
Performs and documents verifications, maintains the credential tracking log and sends renewal notices.
Reviews outside training, validates competency and confirms medication assistance training.
Provides accurate credentials and renews certification on time.

documentation: Caregiver Qualification Checklist
Dated certification verification printouts
Training or competency test documentation
Copies of out-of-state certificates, nursing licenses or proof of graduation
iBudget qualification proof (age, diploma/GED, experience)
Credential tracking log

policies.title: Level 2 Background Screening, Rescreening and Employment History Verification
policies.applies_to: Owners, administrator, alternate administrator, financial officer and every employee or contractor with client contact — Home Health Agency, Homemaker and Companion registrant and nurse registry caregivers
policies.purpose: To protect clients by making sure everyone with access to clients has cleared Level 2 screening and has a verified work history before any client contact.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires Level 2 fingerprint screening, run through the Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse, for owners, the administrator, the financial officer and every employee with client contact before any client contact. Screening is renewed every 5 years through the Clearinghouse. No person with a disqualifying offense under s. 408.809, F.S., may be employed in a screened position or hold any ownership interest, directly or indirectly. When the administrator or alternate administrator changes, Level 2 screening compliance is confirmed and AHCA is notified (Rule 59A-8.0095(1)(b)). Each worker's employment or contractual history is verified with diligent effort, meaning two documented attempts (s. 400.509(4), F.S.; Rule 59A-8.025(7)). The same procedure applies to home health agency hires.

definitions.definition: Fingerprint-based state and national criminal history check required under s. 408.809, F.S.
The Care Provider Background Screening Clearinghouse, where screening results are shared and screening is renewed (s. 435.12, F.S.).
Two documented attempts to verify employment or contractual history; if a number is disconnected, an attempt to find current contact information.
An offense listed in s. 408.809, F.S., that bars employment or ownership unless an exemption is granted.

procedures: Before the hiring offer becomes final, the hiring coordinator tells the applicant that employment is contingent on Level 2 screening, employment verification and the other conditions in PER-01.
The agency maintains an active account and registration in the Clearinghouse. The Administrator designates the staff member who manages it and a backup.
The applicant completes the screening forms, and fingerprints are taken by an approved vendor using the agency's information so results post to the Clearinghouse. The coordinator keeps the receipt.
The coordinator checks the Clearinghouse for results. No applicant has client contact, enters a client home or receives client information until a result showing the person is eligible is on file.

If results show a disqualifying offense, the Administrator does not hire or immediately removes the person from client contact. The agency does not allow work pending an exemption unless the law allows it and the Administrator documents that decision.
The coordinator prints or saves the Clearinghouse eligibility result, dates it, and places it in the personnel file (PER-07).

Owners, the administrator, the alternate administrator and the financial officer are screened at the same standard. The Administrator confirms screening of every owner annually and whenever ownership changes (GOV-07).

When the administrator or alternate administrator changes, the Governing Body ensures the new person has cleared Level 2 screening and notifies AHCA of the change as required (GOV-01). The change is documented in the governance file.

For each applicant, the coordinator verifies prior employment or contractual history for at least the work relevant to caregiving. The first attempt is by phone, email or written request to the former employer or contracting entity.
